The fluorescein angiographic findings include delayed or patchy choroidal filling, delayed arteriovenous filling, and/or prominent vascular staining. Retinal capillaries are typically unaffected.

Choroidal rupture occurs due to sudden compression of the eye along its anterior-posterior axis resulting in a tear in the Bruch membrane and overlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Immediate treatment involves observation.

These discrete atrophic (hypopigmented) spots may occur singly or in clusters. pool.q: Acetazolamide is most beneficial when used to treat cystoid macular edema (CME) associated with what disorder?
pool.rationale:
Unlike CME associated with other etiologies, CME caused by RP may respond to oral acetazolamide treatment.
CME due to CRVO is treated with intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents or steroids.
Vitreomacular traction is treated with surgery or intravitreal ocriplasmin.
Pseudophakic CME typically responds to topical anti-inflammatory treatment.

pool.q: A 22-year-old man presents with night blindness, constricted visual fields, posterior subcapsular cataracts, and cystoid macular edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
This constellation of features is characteristic for retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a heterogeneous group of degenerative retinal disorders that lead to progressive loss of visual function. Affected patients generally complain of night blindness (nyctalopia) and midperipheral scotomas ("ring scotomas") or constriction of their visual fields. Clinical signs of RP include the narrowing of retinal vessels, bone spicule pigmentation within the retina, and waxy pallor of the optic nerve. Some patients may also develop cystoid macular edema and posterior subcapsular cataract.
Cone dystrophy is characterized by the progressive loss of visual acuity, poor color discrimination, and development of a central scotoma. In advanced cases, there may be a localized bilateral macular bull's-eye atrophy pattern or a more diffuse appearance. Vitamin A deficiency and cancer-associated retinopathy present with poor scotopic acuity, constricted visual fields, and variable electroretinogram b-wave amplitude reduction. However, cystoid macular edema and subcapsular cataract are not features associated with either of these conditions.

pool.q: A 19-year-old deaf patient with a known pigmentary retinopathy presents for ptosis repair. His ocular motility is impaired. For what cardiovascular disorder should he be evaluated?
pool.rationale: This patient presents with the constellation of signs of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. This syndrome consists of features of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) plus pigmentary retinopathy. CPEO is associated with heart block, and placement of a cardiac pacemaker may be life-saving. Other features include upgaze limitation, decreased levator function, increased cerebrospinal fluid protein, deafness, vestibular dysfunction, and mitochondrial myopathy with fibers on muscle biopsy. Marfan syndrome is associated with aortic aneurysm and ectopia lentis, but not a pigmentary retinopathy, deafness, or ptosis. Carotid dissection can be traumatic or spontaneous but has no association with CPEO. Congestive heart failure is not associated with CPEO.

pool.q: According to the Branch Vein Occlusion Study, what is the most appropriate initial treatment of a branch retinal vein occlusion in a patient with 20/30 vision but without macular ischemia?

options.b: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor injection

pool.rationale:
The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study (BVOS) predated the use of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal steroids. The BVOS found that laser-treated eyes with intact foveal vasculature, macular edema, and visual acuity in the 20/40–20/200 range were more likely to gain 2 lines of visual acuity (65%) than were untreated eyes (37%). Eyes were observed if visual acuity was better than 20/40. All eyes were observed for at least 3 months to permit the maximum spontaneous resolution of the edema and intraretinal blood.
In the BRAVO trial of intravitreal ranibizumab for branch retinal vein occlusion, eyes with vision better than 20/40 were observed as well.

pool.q: Basal laminar deposits in the retina are a supportive finding in what disease?

Basal laminar deposits are a supportive pathological finding in AMD. They are microscopic deposits between the plasma membrane of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the basement membrane of the RPE.
Pattern dystrophy is a heterogeneous group of inherited macular diseases characterized by varying patterns of pigment deposition at the level of the RPE.
Phototoxicity leads to photoreceptor damage.

pool.q: A healthy 45-year-old woman complains of worsening central vision over the past year. Fundus examination demonstrates symmetric changes as depicted in this image bilaterally.  Fluorescein angiography demonstrates a dark choroid. What test is most appropriate to establish a definitive diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Stargardt disease is an autosomal recessive macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. Patients may present with central vision complaints as early as childhood and as late as age 50, with highly variable phenotypic manifestations. The differential diagnosis includes age-related macular degeneration and hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine retinal toxicity.
A definitive diagnosis can be established by genetic testing. The classic finding of a “silent choroid” on fluorescein angiography is not always present, and the electroretinogram is typically normal. The findings on fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) can exhibit features that overlap with other macular diseases.

pool.q: A 35-year-old man who has been followed by an ophthalmologist for retinitis pigmentosa recently experienced blurred vision. Last year his vision was 20/20 OU, but on examination now his visual acuity is 20/40 OD and 20/20 OS. What is the most likely cause of his central visual loss?
pool.rationale: In this case of asymmetric mild vision loss in RP from 20/20 to 20/40, the most likely cause is cystoid macular edema. Alternatives include development of a posterior subcapsular cataract or advanced constriction of the midperipheral and peripheral loss. Secondary glaucoma only has a weak association with RP and would not be responsible for a mild decrease in central vision. Cystoid macular edema from RP can be treated with oral acetazaolamide or intravitreal triamcinolone. However, treatment-resistant CME in RP is common.

pool.q: In a patient with postoperative serous choroidal detachment, what additional feature might an ophthalmologist expect to find?

options.c: most elevated over the vortex vein ampullae

pool.rationale: Postoperative serous choroidal detachments after a glaucoma filtering procedure are generally associated with hypotony. They are more common in myopes than hyperopes, and are painless in contrast to hemorrhagic choroidal detachments, which are typically painful. Most serous choroidal detachments resolve spontaneously or, in rare cases, may require revision of the glaucoma-filtering procedure to reduce hypotony. Rarely will persistent choroidal detachment require surgical drainage. pool.q: What systemic condition has the highest association frequency with branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO)?

pool.q: What condition represents the most common indication for scleral buckle surgery?
pool.rationale: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment represents the most common indication for scleral buckle surgery. This procedure is not indicated for the primary management of choroidal effusion, exudative retinal detachment, or proliferative diabetic retinopathy. pool.q: What is the characteristic clinical feature of primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis?
pool.rationale: Retinal vascular sheathing is a common clinical feature of primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis. Although hypopyon iritis may occur along with retinal vasculitis in Behçet disease, it is not a common finding in primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis. Subretinal hemorrhage and retinal neovascularization are also not common findings in primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis.

pool.q: On dilated fundus examination, a 41-year-old emmetropic, phakic woman is incidentally found to have an operculated hole. She has no associated lattice degeneration and no prior history of retinal detachment. What is the best treatment option for this patient?

However, asymptomatic flap tears accompanied by lattice degeneration, myopia, subclinical detachment, aphakia, pseudophakia, or a history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye have an increased risk of retinal detachment, and treatment may be considered. Asymptomatic operculated holes and atrophic holes rarely cause retinal detachment and therefore treatment is not generally recommended.

pool.q: What is the typical appearance of adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy?

options.a: bilateral, coarse pigment mottling in central macula
options.c: bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions
options.d: bilateral fishnet pattern of yellow-orange or brown pigment

Adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy presents as bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions.
Bilateral, butterfly-shaped, yellow macular pigment is seen in butterfly-type pattern dystrophy.
Fishnet pattern of yellow-orange or brown pigment is seen in reticular dystrophy.
Coarse pigment mottling in central macula is seen in fundus pulverulentus.

pool.q: A 23-year-old athletic male complains of decreased vision in the upper visual field of his left eye. Examination reveals a retinal dialysis from 4 to 6:30 o'clock associated with a shallow inferior retinal detachment just posterior to the equator. What is the preferred treatment?

options.a: Schedule a scleral buckle procedure for the next available time.
options.b: Schedule vitrectomy, internal drainage, laser demarcation, and C3F8 gas injection for the next available time.
options.d: Perform emergent vitrectomy, internal drainage, laser demarcation, and C3F8 gas injection.

pool.rationale:
Retinal dialyses are notorious for delayed presentation of associated retinal detachments. Because this patient’s detachment is inferior and distant from the macula, the urgency of this situation is moderated. Retinal detachments associated with retinal dialyses have very high reattachment rates with scleral buckle procedures. When performed in the absence of a pars plana vitrectomy, scleral buckle procedures utilize retinal cryopexy to create chorioretinal adhesions around any retinal breaks, with or without external drainage of subretinal fluid. This approach has the advantage of avoiding the need for a gas bubble which would promote cataractogenesis in this young phakic patient.
In the event that vitrectomy, laser, and gas injection were considered, a shorter duration gas such as SF6 would be preferred, to avoid prolonged need for eye down positioning. Vitrectomy is the preferred surgical option, over scleral buckle with retinal cryopexy, in cases with giant retinal tears, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, poorly defined breaks, or pseudophakic patients in whom it is uncertain that all breaks have been identified. Observation of a symptomatic retinal detachment is contraindicated.

pool.q: A patient presents with a suspected open-globe injury from a construction accident. The patient is unsure what hit his eye. Vision from the eye is light perception only. External examination reveals a total hyphema and 360 degrees of subconjunctival hemorrhage. The patient has not had anything to eat or drink in at least 8 hours. What is the best next step in management?

options.a: immediate globe exploration in the operating room
options.b: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits
options.c: computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain and orbits
options.d: placement of a fox shield on the eye and a plan for immediate globe exploration and possible repair of open globe

pool.rationale: The first step in a suspected open-globe injury should be a CT scan of the brain and orbits. A CT scan will evaluate the shape of the globe and help identify an intraocular foreign body (IOFB). Additionally, it can identify other head and facial trauma. MRI is helpful for identifying wood or glass foreign bodies that may be difficult to detect on CT. However, if a metallic foreign body is suspected, as in this case in a construction accident, MRI should be avoided, because movement of a metallic IOFB could cause additional damage. Although immediate globe exploration in the operating room can be performed, it is inferior to CT scan and risks causing extrusion of ocular contents. While this patient will almost certainly need surgery, imaging should be performed first, as the findings may impact the surgical plan.

pool.q: In an eye with retinoschisis, what examination findings are associated with an increased risk of progression to retinal detachment?
pool.rationale: The presence of inner and outer layer breaks in retinoschisis is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. However, the presence of outer layer breaks (but not inner breaks) can lead to a localized retinal detachment that usually does not progress and seldom requires treatment. The presence of a bullous inner layer does not predispose to retinal detachment. Finally, the presence of a demarcation line in an eye with retinoschisis indicates that a chronic localized retinal detachment is present or has spontaneously regressed; this is not likely to lead to a progressive retinal detachment.

pool.q: A 40-year-old man presents with an active focal retinochoroiditis with an adjacent retinochoroidal scar. The patient recalls no prior episodes of uveitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The vast majority of ocular toxoplasmosis is acquired. The presence of a retinochoroidal scar is strong support for prior infection, meaning that this particular episode is not primary and that infection could have occurred either at or long after birth. The absence of an adjacent or nearby retinochoroidal scar together with a positive serum test result for anti-Toxoplasma gondii IgM antibody would constitute strong supportive evidence for an acutely acquired infection. Cytomegalovirus retinitis is rare and is typically observed in severely immunosuppressed individuals.

pool.q: For this asymptomatic, 35-year-old man with a corrected visual acuity of 20/20 OU and the fundus shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The image demonstrates macular drusen. In an asymptomatic 35-year-old patient, the most likely diagnosis is familial dominant drusen, which could be confirmed by examination of first-degree relatives. Other less likely diagnoses would include cuticular drusen (basal laminar drusen), Sorsby macular dystrophy, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type 2, or malattia leventinese (radial drusen, Doyne macular dystrophy, or mutation in EFEMP1). A minimum age cutoff of 50 years is usually used to differentiate age-related macular degeneration from the earlier presenting phenotypes. Adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (pattern dystrophy) is characterized by the presence of more discrete, localized macular lesions unlike the diffuse drusen demonstrated in the image. The flecks associated with Stargardt disease tend to be less diffuse than familial dominant drusen. In addition, a 35-year-old patient with Stargardt disease would, in general, have a reduction in visual acuity.

pool.q: For the condition illustrated, what is the most common associated systemic condition?
pool.rationale: The image demonstrates retinitis and retinal hemorrhage from cytomegalovirus. This condition is most commonly associated with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. It can also result from immune suppression caused by chemotherapy or as required for organ transplantation. Antiviral therapy, typically with oral valganciclovir, is indicated for the treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis. If HIV is found, additional systemic highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) should be initiated.

pool.q: A patient presents with a decline in vision in the right eye. The fundus appearance is shown below. What patient characteristic is more commonly associated with this condition?
pool.rationale: This patient is presenting with a macular hole. For the majority of patients with macular hole, the cause is unknown or idiopathic. For the remainder of patients, myopia and direct blunt ocular trauma are associated characteristics. Idiopathic holes are most prevalent in patients from 50 to 80 years of age and are more common in women.

pool.q: What fluorescein angiographic feature would be seen in a patient with an episode of acute, severe hypertension who eventually develops the lesions shown in the figure?

options.a: at least 10 disc areas of retinal capillary nonperfusion
options.b: progressive irregular hyperfluorescence at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
options.c: collateral vessels which do not leak and have large caliber
options.d: early choroidal hypoperfusion followed by multiple subretinal areas of leakage in the late phases

Hypertension may lead to hypertensive retinopathy, choroidopathy, and/or optic neuropathy. The image shows Elschnig spots, which develop from lobular nonperfusion of the choriocapillaris that eventually becomes hyperpigmented and surrounded by margins of hypopigmentation, indicating hypertensive choroidopathy.
Choroidal involvement includes fluorescein angiographic findings of early-phase focal choroidal hypoperfusion and late multiple subretinal areas of leakage. Progressive irregular hyperfluorescence at the level of the RPE occurs in acute idiopathic maculopathy. Collateral vessels have a larger caliber and do not leak on fluorescein angiography (FA). pool.q: What is the appropriate management of an asymptomatic patient with lattice degeneration without breaks?

options.a: a discussion of the warning signs of retinal detachment
options.b: regular follow-up examinations 2 to 3 times a year
options.c: prophylactic laser treatment to all areas of lattice degeneration

pool.rationale:
Lattice degeneration without any breaks can be safely observed; however, the patient should be made aware of the need for prompt evaluation if there are signs or symptoms of retinal tear or retinal detachment.
Prophylactic laser or scleral buckle is not required in an asymptomatic patient with lattice degeneration. These patients can be followed with annual examinations.

pool.q: What feature of the choroid mitigates the potential thermal damage associated with light absorption?
pool.rationale: The high speed of blood flow through the choroid helps to dissipate thermal energy from light absorption in addition to maintaining the oxygen needs of the photoreceptors (and resulting in high oxygen tension in venous blood). The multilayer arterial structure of the choroid, which is thicker centrally than peripherally, allows blood to be delivered across the extent of the retina, with an accompanying decrease in pressure before reaching the choriocapillaris.

pool.q: In a premature infant born at 29 weeks’ gestation, what is the appropriate time for the initial screening examination for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
pool.rationale: Screening should be done on all infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g or a gestational age of 30 weeks or less. The first examination should generally be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of postnatal age or, alternatively, between 31 and 33 weeks’ postconceptional or postmenstrual age, whichever is later. In this case the infant is born at 29 weeks, hence the first examination should be done 4 to 6 weeks after birth.

pool.q: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows a well-circumscribed intraconal mass with uniform enhancement indenting the posterior globe. What funduscopic finding is expected?
pool.rationale:
An intraconal mass can cause pressure on the posterior globe, leading to choroidal folds. Another cause of choroidal folds from external forces is thyroid eye disease. Other causes of choroidal folds include posterior scleritis, choroidal infiltration from lymphoma, hypotony, and a poorly characterized condition in which middle-aged adults develop symmetric choroidal folds bilaterally. Localized choroidal folds can be seen in association with choroidal neovascularization, choroidal neoplasms, and scleral buckles.

Patton lines are fine folds that course circumferentially around the optic nerve head in the setting of increased intracranial pressure. Papilledema is optic nerve swelling secondary to increased intracranial pressure, which would not be expected from an intraconal mass. Choroidal thickness is inversely related to degree of myopia and increasing age; subretinal drusenoid deposits also increase the risk of geographic atrophy. Choroidal atrophy would not be expected to occur secondary to an orbital mass.

pool.q: A 19-year-old man developed an acute reduction in central vision, a central scotoma, and a yellow spot in his central macula. What drug may lead to this presentation?
pool.rationale: “Poppers” is a slang term for alkyl nitrites, which are a class of chemical used as recreational drugs. The chemicals are inhaled to induce euphoria and relax smooth muscles, usually in preparation for sexual activity. In rare cases, use can lead to acute central scotoma and vision reduction associated with a yellow, “vitelliform”-like macular lesion. In rare cases, MEK inhibitors, which are a class of chemotherapeutic agents, and sildenafil have been associated with serous macular fluid, which may simulate central serous choroidopathy. Corticosteroids may precipitate serous exudation from central serous retinopathy.

pool.q: A law student presents to the emergency department for evaluation of “blurry vision,” and is noted to have bilateral serous retinal detachments with whitish dots underneath the retinal surface on examination. The most likely diagnosis in this scenario has been associated with use of what class of medication?
pool.rationale: The most likely diagnosis in this case, suggested by bilateral serous retinal detachments with "white dots" under the retina, is central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), which has been associated with corticosteroid use. pool.q: What is an indication for prompt surgical intervention in the setting of a visually significant vitreous hemorrhage secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy?

options.a: extramacular traction retinal detachment demonstrated on B-scan ultrasonography
options.b: attached posterior vitreous hyaloid demonstrated on B-scan ultrasonography
options.c: dense vitreous hemorrhage precluding visualization of posterior segment on indirect ophthalmoscopy
options.d: poor visual acuity in the fellow eye secondary to complications of proliferative diabetic retinopathy

pool.q: What represents the most common mechanism of traumatic avulsion of the optic nerve?

options.a: penetrating globe injury, causing a sudden decompression injury
options.b: penetrating orbital injury, causing a forward pull on the optic nerve
options.c: extreme rotation and rearward displacement of the globe
options.d: sudden increase in IOP, causing rupture of the lamina cribrosa

pool.rationale: Sudden increase in IOP, causing rupture of the lamina cribrosa, represents the most common mechanism of traumatic avulsion of the optic nerve. Extreme rotation and/or forward displacement of the globe, and penetrating orbital injury causing a rearward pull on the optic nerve, are other potential mechanisms. Penetrating globe injury, causing a sudden decompression injury, is not a cause of this condition.

pool.q: A 68-year-old man reports a "missing spot" in his vision 1 week following cataract extraction by a first-year resident. Best corrected visual acuity is 20/100. In addition to normal postoperative findings, the examination is significant only for subtle foveal hypopigmentation. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrates the findings shown in the photo. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Nonexudative age-related macular degeneration, macular holes, and epiretinal membranes can all decrease central visual acuity; however, in the setting of recent (and likely prolonged) ophthalmic surgery with this supporting OCT, photic retinopathy secondary to exposure to the operating microscope light source is the most likely diagnosis. pool.q: A 32-year-old hyperope is referred for a second opinion regarding refractory central serous choroidopathy. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes subretinal fluid. There are no anterior chamber or vitreous cell abnormalities, and the patient reports no pain. A fluorescein angiogram reveals a "leopard spot" pattern of hyperfluorescence as shown. These findings indicate that the original diagnosis was incorrect. What is the correct diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Uveal effusion syndrome is characterized by impaired posterior segment drainage, causing exudative detachment of the retina, choroid, or ciliary body. Young age, hyperopia, and nanophthalmos are risk factors. It can be mistakenly diagnosed as central serous choroidopathy. Examination findings include shifting subretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) hypertrophy. A fluorescein angiogram reveals a characteristic leopard spot appearance.
MEWDS does not typically present with exudative retinal or choroidal detachment. Although VKH can include exudative fluid and RPE changes, it typically includes a uveitic component, as well as constitutional signs, such as vitiligo and poliosis. Posterior scleritis would typically be painful.

pool.q: When treating the patient shown, which pharmaceutical agent is considered a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor analog or “VEGF trap”?
pool.rationale: The image demonstrates exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Current therapies for exudative AMD are directed at inhibiting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the cytokine most strongly implicated in the development of choroidal neovascularization. Aflibercept (Eylea) is nonspecific VEGF receptor analog referred to as VEGF trap. Ranibizumab (Lucentis) and bevacizumab (Avastin) bind to all isoforms of VEGF and are therefore nonspecific inhibitors of VEGF. Pegaptanib (Macugen) is an aptamer that binds to VEGF isoform 165.

pool.q: In a patient presenting with acute, symptomatic posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with vitreous hemorrhage, what is the chance that a retinal tear is present?
pool.rationale: Overall, 7%-18% of patients with acute, symptomatic PVD have retinal tears. However, 50%-70% of patients with acute PVD and vitreous hemorrhage have retinal tears. The risk of retinal tears in 7%-12% in patients with acute PVD without vitreous hemorrhage.

pool.q: What laboratory test should be performed in all black patients presenting with a traumatic hyphema?
pool.rationale: Sickle cell disease is an important risk factor for hyphema among persons of African descent. In the setting of high intraocular pressure (IOP) from hyphema and sickle cell disease, IOP-lowering medications, such as acetazolamide, would be relatively contraindicated, as they may precipitate a sickle cell crisis. A hypercoagulable state may lead to bleeding in the retina due to vascular occlusion, but it is not associated with hyphema.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of decreased visual acuity in patients who present with acute central retinal vein occlusion?
pool.rationale: Patients with acute central retinal vein occlusion commonly present with reduced visual acuity secondary to macular edema. Neovascularization of the iris usually occurs 3 to 5 months after the onset of symptoms. Peripheral ischemia with capillary dropout is seen in some severe cases of central retinal vein occlusion and can promote neovascularization, resulting in vitreous hemorrhage. Macular ischemia can occur as well but is a less likely cause of decreased acuity on presentation.

pool.q: An 80-year-old patient with painless vision loss has the finding pictured. What blood work is necessary in the initial evaluation?
pool.rationale:
The image shows a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). No embolus can be seen.  Giant cell arteritis is the etiology of CRAO in 1%-2% of cases. Undetected and untreated, it represents a significant risk factor for second-eye involvement, with potentially devastating consequences. As such, an ESR should be obtained in all patients presenting with a CRAO.

pool.q: Which eyes are at greatest risk for the development of an RPE tear after anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy?

options.c: eyes with a fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment (PED) > 600 µm in height

pool.q: A 60-year-old reports gradual vision loss in the left eye and aching pain localized to the left orbit. pool.q: A 70-year-old man with poor visual acuity since childhood comes for a routine exam. His visual acuity is 20/200. X-linked inheritance is implied by the family history, because the patient’s daughter would be an obligate carrier and her sons would have a 50% chance of being affected. Mild trauma in boys with XLRS can cause vitreous hemorrhage related to shearing of vessels in areas of peripheral retinoschisis. The history and clinical features in this patient are thus suggestive of XLRS.

In addition, pigmentary deposits are classically located around the arcades rather than more peripherally and patients can maintain good central visual acuity. Retinitis pigmentosa, which can be X-linked, is not accompanied by an electronegative ERG. Finally, although advanced Best disease may be characterized by poor visual acuity and macular atrophy, peripheral pigmentation is absent and the ERG is normal.

pool.q: What clinical finding best characterizes Coats disease?

pool.q: The macular lesion shown is characteristic of what disorder?

Sorsby pseudoinflammatory fundus dystrophy is characterized by progressive degeneration of the central macula with edema, hemorrhage, exudate, and pigment changes.

pool.q: What is the main glycosaminoglycan component of vitreous?
pool.rationale: Hyaluronan (hyaluronic acid) is the main glycosaminoglycan found in vitreous. Other major components include water and collagen. Although dermatan, chondroitin, and keratan are glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), they are not the principal GAGs found in the vitreous.

Eales disease is an occlusive vasculitis associated with extraretinal neovascularization and occurs at highest prevalence in regions of endemic tuberculosis because there may be an associated tuberculin hypersensitivity.
Sickle cell anemia is associated with presence of abnormal hemoglobin and is not associated with tuberculosis.
IRVAN and incontinentia pigmenti are not associated with tuberculosis.

pool.q: What is the reported incidence of central nervous system hemangiomas in patients with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease?
pool.rationale: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is an autosomal dominantly inherited disorder caused by a mutation in the tumor suppressor gene, the VHL gene. The clinical manifestations included benign and malignant tumors of the retina, central nervous system, kidneys, adrenal gland, meninges, and cysts of the pancreas, kidney, liver, inner ear, epididymis, and broad ligament of the uterus. Central nervous system hemangiomas have been reported in 20% of patients.

pool.q: What bilateral white dot syndrome is characterized by profound vision loss typically followed by full or near-full vision recovery?

options.a: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

pool.rationale: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is an uncommon, usually bilateral inflammatory disorder characterized by acute onset visual loss, usually followed weeks to months later by substantial or near-complete improvement. On FA, APMPPE (also known as AMPPE or AMPPPE) in the acute phase demonstrates a characteristic fundus pattern of early lesion blockage, followed by lesion staining in the middle and late phases. No treatment has been demonstrated to affect the time or final outcome of recovery. Birdshot uveitis is characterized by insidious onset and chronic progression. Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a unilateral syndrome with decreased vision, scotomas, and sometimes photopsias, with improvement over 2-6 weeks without treatment. Serpiginous chorioretinopathy is typically relentlessly progressive, and destroys the RPE on photoreceptors. Thus, recovery of vision, even following immunosuppression, is atypical.

pool.q: What is the predominant mode of inheritance of Stargardt disease/fundus flavimaculatus?
pool.rationale: Stargardt disease is the most common juvenile macular dystrophy and a common cause of central vision loss in adults younger than 50 years. The visual acuity in Stargardt disease typically ranges from 20/50 to 20/200. The classic Stargardt phenotype is characterized by a juvenile-onset foveal atrophy surrounded by discrete, yellowish, round or pisciform flecks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The vast majority of Stargardt disease is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. This includes those cases caused by mutations in an adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP)-binding cassette transporter protein (ABCA4). Rarer forms of Stargardt disease may be inherited as an autosomal dominant pattern (PRPH2).

pool.q: What is a meridional fold?

options.a: redundant retinal tissue that extends radially into the pars plana
options.b: a peripheral area of retinal pigment epithelial cell proliferation at the level of the vitreous base
options.c: a peripheral, focal area of elevated glial hyperplasia
options.d: a posterior extension of the pars plana into retina

pool.rationale:
A meridional fold is redundant retinal tissue that extends radially into the pars plana. It is often located superonasally. Meridional folds increase the risk of retinal detachment.
An ora bay is a posterior extension of the pars plana into retina. Vitreoretinal tufts are peripheral, focal areas of elevated glial hyperplasia associated with vitreous or zonular attachment and traction. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) proliferation or hyperplasia may occur in areas of chronic, low-grade traction on the retina.

pool.q: Concerned parents of a 5-year-old child who was recently found to have Coats disease would like to know about the genetic risk factors for it. What is the inheritance pattern of this disease?
pool.rationale: Coats disease is an idiopathic condition characterized by telangiectatic and aneurysmal retinal vessels. It is considered sporadic because there is no evidence to suggest genetic transmission of Coats disease. To date no gene or chromosome has been associated with this disease, and there has been no identifiable hereditary pattern; however, there is a marked male predominance of cases observed (85%).

pool.q: What is the most likely mechanism for sudden loss of vision associated with sickle cell retinopathy?
pool.rationale: Sickle cell retinopathy can cause visual symptoms for a number of reasons, including vitreous hemorrhage, macular ischemia, vascular occlusions, and retinal detachment. Visual symptoms are most frequently caused by vitreous hemorrhage derived from the retinal neovascularization. Occlusive vascular changes and an enlarged foveal avascular zone (FAZ) are common in patients with sickle cell retinopathy but may not produce symptoms. Retinal detachments, whether rhegmatogenous, tractional, or combined, can occur but are not the most common cause of visual symptoms.

pool.q: In patients with lattice degeneration who do not receive prophylactic treatment, what percentage will have a retinal detachment in the affected eye?
pool.rationale: Half of patients with lattice degeneration have concomitant atrophic retinal holes. In contrast to this high prevalence, only 1% to 2% of patients with atrophic retinal holes later develop a clinical retinal detachment.

pool.q: For a patient with lattice degeneration, what is the strongest additional indication for treating with laser retinopexy and/or cryopexy?

options.a: symptomatic retinal tear with or without a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)
options.c: asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes with limited surrounding subretinal fluid and a prominent demarcation line surrounding the fluid and lattice
options.d: asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes without surrounding subretinal fluid

pool.rationale: A symptomatic retinal tear would convey the highest risk of retinal detachment and would therefore be the strongest indication for laser retinopexy and/or cryopexy in a patient with lattice degeneration whether with or without a precipitating PVD. Asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes without surrounding subretinal fluid, asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes with limited surrounding subretinal fluid and a prominent demarcation line, and multiple rows of lattice degeneration without retinal breaks represent lower-risk situations for progression to clinical retinal detachment. Treatment is rarely indicated in these circumstances. A history of retinal detachment in the other eye that was caused by a lattice related tear or atrophic hole may increase the appropriateness to treat lattice lesions with atrophic holes with or without fluid.

pool.q: A diabetic patient with normal vision is found to have a moderate number of microaneurysms and intraretinal hemorrhages in the macula and periphery of each retina. There is no evidence of macular edema on clinical examination or on optical coherence tomography (OCT), nor is there neovascularization or other vascular abnormalities. What is an appropriate recommendation for management of this patient's condition?

options.d: consumption of 81 mg of aspirin per day

pool.rationale: The clinical presentation is consistent with moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) without macular edema. Optimization of glycemic control has been shown to slow the progression of disease at this stage. The 2019 AAO Preferred Practice Pattern does not advise fluorescein angiography (FA) as part of the regular examination of diabetic patients. In patients with severe NPDR or proliferative diabetic retinopathy, however, FA can be a valuable tool in indicating the severity of retinal ischemia and identifying clinically occult neovascularization. Neither prophylactic scatter laser photocoagulation nor low-dose aspirin has been proven to benefit this disease stage.

pool.q: A 22-year-old man experiences sudden pain and blurred vision while mowing his lawn. Examination reveals visual acuity of 20/40, a small conjunctival hemorrhage over the temporal pars plana region, a quiet anterior chamber, clear lens, and mild temporal and inferior vitreous hemorrhage. Ultrasonography reveals a small, highly reflective object in the inferior vitreous. What is the best next step in managing this patient's condition?

options.a: frequent topical antibiotic and steroid administration with close follow-up
options.b: pars plana vitrectomy with removal of the foreign body
options.c: magnetic extraction of the foreign body in the minor procedure room
options.d: vitreous tap with injection of vancomycin and ceftazidime

pool.rationale: This patient's clinical history is consistent with a penetrating ocular injury by a retained intraocular foreign body. Management consists of pars plana vitrectomy, foreign body removal, repair of associated injuries (scleral laceration, traumatic cataract, retinal tear, etc.), and administration of intravitreal antibiotics. This treatment regimen is most safely and effectively performed in the controlled setting of the operating room.

pool.q: A 29-year-old man presents for routine ophthalmic examination. He notes poor vision in his left eye for "as long as he can remember," but he has never had an eye examination in the past. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye is unremarkable. Fundus examination of the left eye is depicted in the figure. What would a fluorescein angiogram, if performed, be most likely to demonstrate?

options.b: no leakage, as well as a gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation
options.d: hyperfluorescence secondary to diffuse leakage throughout the lesion

pool.rationale:
The figure depicts a retinal cavernous hemangioma, which is a benign hamartoma. Most cases are sporadic, although a familial, autosomal dominant pattern has been seen in conjunction with skin and intracranial hemangiomas. Clinically, a retinal cavernous hemangioma appears as a grape-like cluster of thin-walled saccular angiomatous lesions in the inner retina or optic nerve. They are typically located peripherally and are asymptomatic (this patient has a severe case involving the central vision that is less common). Rarely, the hemangiomas may bleed into the vitreous. This lesion should be on the differential diagnosis of any patient with a vitreous hemorrhage of unknown etiology. In addition, cavernous hemangiomas are one of the conditions that can cause subretinal, intraretinal, and preretinal hemorrhage. Blood flow through the lesions is slow.
Fluorescein angiography typically shows no leakage and may show gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation. Subretinal edema and exudate is uncommon. Most lesions are observed unless they cause vision loss, in which case cryotherapy or photocoagulation may be considered. If severe vitreous hemorrhage occurs, pars plana vitrectomy is an option.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with blurry vision, and the ophthalmologist identifies a large inferior bullous detachment. The overlying retinal surface is smooth. The patient is placed into a reclining position to allow more careful examination of the periphery, and at the conclusion of the negative sclera-depression examination, the ophthalmologist notes that now the posterior pole is detached. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this condition?

options.d: work-up for underlying malignancy or inflammatory disorder

pool.rationale: Vascular, malignant, and inflammatory disorders are the most common causes of exudative retinal detachment, which is the diagnosis in this case. As such, identification and treatment of the underlying cause represents the primary management of this disorder. Exudative detachments are characterized by a smooth retinal surface and subretinal fluid that shifts with head position, as in this case. Management is typically nonsurgical.

pool.q: By what inheritance pattern is Stargardt disease transmitted?
pool.rationale: Stargardt disease (SD) is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. SD results from mutations in the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter ABCA4 (ABCR), one of the largest and most polymorphous genes known. Abnormal ABCA4 (ABCR) protein function is thought to lead to the accumulation of lipofuscin in the retinal pigment epithelium, limiting its function and viability.

pool.q: The risk of hemorrhagic choroidal detachment during or after intraocular surgery is increased by what finding?
pool.rationale:
Hypertension is a reported risk factor for hemorrhagic choroidal detachment; others include low intraocular pressure during surgery, advanced age, and myopia.
Elevated intraocular pressure during surgery, younger age, and hyperopia do not increase the risk of hemorrhagic choroidal detachment. Reported risk factors are:
  • advanced age
  • aphakia
  • myopia
  • arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease
  • hypertension
  • hypotony (transient)
  • glaucoma
  • Sturge-Weber-associated choroidal hemangiomas
  • tachycardia (intraoperative)

pool.q: What is the most common complication of type 1 juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasis?
pool.rationale: The most common complication of type 1 juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasis is macular edema. Although retinal neovascularization may complicate this condition, it is less common than macular edema. Retinal tears and vitreous hemorrhage are not typically associated with type 1 juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasis.

pool.q: A 78-year-old man trips and falls on a sidewalk, and his right eye is injured by the teeth of a rake. He has a 360-degree dense subconjunctival hemorrhage, intraocular pressure of 8, and a peaked pupil. What is the primary concern in this situation?

options.b: vitreous prolapse into the anterior chamber
options.d: uveal prolapse indicating an open globe

pool.rationale: The primary concern in this patient is for an open-globe injury, given the 360-degree hemorrhage and the peaked pupil. The other choices (hypotony causing suprachoroidal hemorrhage, retinal detachment causing uveal shift, vitreous prolapse into the anterior chamber) are possibly present in addition, but one must rule out an open injury.

pool.q: What clinical feature is most suggestive of Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis?

options.a: inflammatory cellular aggregates in the vitreous ("fluff balls")
options.b: white plaque within the lens capsule

pool.rationale: A white plaque within the lens capsule following cataract surgery is associated with Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis. P acnes endophthalmitis is typically characterized by chronic, indolent, granulomatous inflammation. This infection is rarely eradicated with an intracapsular antibiotic injection or intravitreal antibiotic injection alone and typically requires pars plana vitrectomy with partial capsulectomy in addition to intracapsular antibiotic deposition. Diffuse stellate keratic precipitates, hypopyon mixed with hyphema, and inflammatory cellular aggregates in the vitreous ("fluff balls") are not typically associated with Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis.

pool.q: Retinal telangiectasis of Coats disease is most commonly found in what location?
pool.rationale: Changes in vasculature in Coats disease are most often seen in the peripheral retina, although any portion of the peripheral and macular capillary system may be involved.

pool.q: What finding most supports a working diagnosis of ocular toxoplasmosis infection?

options.a: a peripheral granuloma with a tractional band that extends towards the macula
options.b: acute focal chorioretinitis adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar
options.c: a choroidal neovascular membrane adjacent to a chorioretinal scar
options.d: clusters of gray-white or yellow-white outer retinal and choroidal lesions.

pool.rationale:
Acute focal chorioretinitis adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar supports a working diagnosis of ocular toxoplasmosis infection. Positive serum IgG antibody titer is only indicative of previous exposure to T gondii (recent or past), and is not specific for active disease. T gondii is a protozoan, not a bacterium, and is not typically isolable from a vitreous specimen.
A peripheral granuloma with a tractional band that extends toward the macula is typical of toxocariasis. A choroidal neovascular membrane adjacent to a chorioretinal scar is more typical of ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. Clusters of gray-white or yellow-white outer retinal and choroidal lesions may be seen in the acute phase of diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN).

pool.q: A patient develops branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) at a site other than an arteriovenous crossing. What underlying etiology should be considered?
pool.rationale: In branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), obstruction of the vein occurs most commonly at an arteriovenous crossing, where thickening of the arterial wall compresses the adjacent vein within a common adventitial sheath. When the occlusion does not occur at an arteriovenous crossing, the possibility of an underlying retinochoroiditis or retinal vasculitis should be considered. Hypertension and glaucoma are risk factors for BRVO but are not implicated in occlusion at sites other than arteriovenous crossings. An embolus may cause a retinal artery occlusion but not a retinal vein occlusion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is most commonly seen in what disease (from most to least common)?
pool.rationale:
Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is most commonly seen with SC > SThal > SS disease. Sickle cell results from a defective allele of hemoglobin A. In SC disease, the valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta-polypeptide chain. Peripheral arteriolar occlusion and capillary nonperfusion of the retina may occur, which may lead to peripheral "sea-fan" retinal neovascularization at the border of perfused and nonperfused retina. Treatment is laser photocoagulation to areas of ischemic retina. However, treatment is not recommended directly to "sea fans," as retinal tears and hemorrhage may result.
Complications of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy include vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. Nonproliferative sickle cell retinopathy may present as salmon-patch hemorrhages (intraretinal hemorrhage after arteriolar occlusion), refractile/iridescent deposits (resorbed hemorrhage with hemosiderin deposits within the inner retina), or black sunburst lesions (retinal pigment epithelium [RPE] hypertrophy/hyperplasia from prior hemorrhage). In addition, patients can develop spontaneous vascular occlusions of large retinal arteries. Another eye finding is the "comma sign." Many comma-shaped thrombi dilate and occlude the conjunctival capillaries. They are most commonly seen in the inferior bulbar conjunctiva. Similarly, segmentation of blood vessels may be seen on the optic disc as the "disc sign."
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What surgical procedure is most indicated for a total retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and multiple posterior retinal breaks?
pool.rationale: Pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle, membrane peeling to relieve traction, retinectomy in case of incarceration or retinal shortening, flattening retina by air or perfluorocarbon liquid, laser or cryoretinopexy, and gas or silicone oil tamponade, is indicated for a total retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and multiple posterior retinal breaks. Pneumatic retinopexy is contraindicated in the presence of PVR. Laser demarcation is not effective for a total retinal detachment. Scleral buckle alone is typically not effective in the presence of multiple posterior retinal breaks.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When attempting to diagnose a circumscribed choroidal hemangioma, what confirming feature can be found most consistently?

options.b: late-phase hypofluorescence on indocyanine green angiography

pool.rationale: Circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas are among the rarest intraocular tumors. In Sturge-Weber disease, choroidal hemangiomas may be diffuse and typically have a tomato ketchup appearance. For circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas, the color can vary from white to red, depending on the overlying RPE. On indocyanine green angiography, persistent diffuse hyperfluorescence might be apparent in the late phase. Serous retinal detachments can be associated with choroidal hemangiomas, but they are usually less severe than those that occur with malignant melanoma of the choroid. Echography of circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas usually demonstrates a highly reflective mass with uniform, high internal spikes; this feature is the most consistent finding.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an important risk factor for ocular toxoplasmosis?

options.a: living in the Ohio River Valley

pool.rationale: Consumption of undercooked or raw meat or of substances contaminated with cat feces are risk factors for ocular toxoplasmosis. Exposure to ticks increases the risk of Lyme disease, whereas exposure to mosquitoes increases the risk of acquiring various infectious disease–causing organisms (eg, the parasites that cause malaria or the West Nile virus). The Ohio River Valley is endemic for the ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.

pool.q: By definition, a giant retinal tear extends at least how many clock-hours?
pool.rationale: Giant retinal tears extend at least 3 clock-hours (90°) circumferentially. These tears typically occur at the posterior edge of the vitreous base.

pool.q: By what mechanism can nicotinic acid affect vision?
pool.rationale:
Niacin can cause cystoid macular edema that shows lack of fluorescein leakage into the cyst-like spaces.
Amiodarone causes cornea verticillata and optic neuropathy. 
Hydroxychloroquine toxicity causes bull's-eye maculopathy.

pool.q: The use of what compound can cause inner segment ellipsoid disruption apparent on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) imaging?
pool.rationale: Alkyl nitrite inhalation has been associated with central disruption of the inner segment ellipsoid layer on SD-OCT analysis, sometimes referred to as poppers maculopathy. Ingestion of kola nuts or canthaxanthine or injection of talc can cause a crystalline maculopathy.

pool.q: What disorder is characteristically associated with a negative ERG waveform?
pool.rationale: A negative ERG waveform refers to a preserved a-wave and a selectively reduced b-wave; it can be present in several clinical diseases including CSNB, X-linked retinoschisis, paraneoplastic retinopathy, and central retinal artery occlusion.

pool.q: What condition may mimic age-related degenerative retinoschisis?
pool.rationale: Degenerative retinoschisis can be confused with a chronic retinal detachment because the retina may appear smooth and thin. Unlike retinoschisis, however, chronic retinal detachments are associated with a retinal break and demarcation lines. Hemorrhagic choroidal detachments, choroidal malignant melanomas, and age-related macular degeneration are unlikely to be confused with degenerative retinoschisis.

pool.q: A one-year-old boy presents with peripheral traction retinal detachment with temporal displacement of the maculae bilaterally. The child's father is similarly affected. There is no history of premature birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) occurs in full-term infants and is characterized by exudative leakage and hemorrhage of the blood vessels of the temporal peripheral retina, along with incomplete vascularization of the peripheral retina. This may result in contraction of fibrovascular tissue with the development of a traction retinal detachment (TRD). The condition may be inherited in an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or x-linked pattern. Congenital retinal telangiectasia and juvenile retinoschisis are not typically associated with a TRD. Incontinentia pigmenti is typically lethal in male infants.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the best treatment for atrophic retinal holes?
pool.rationale:
Patients with atrophic retinal holes are at low risk for developing a retinal detachment, but they should be made aware of the need for prompt evaluation if new floaters or photopsias develop.
Asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes pose a low risk for retinal detachment and can be safely observed. Laser treatment reduces risk of retinal detachment but does not eliminate it. New tears can develop at the edge of a previous laser scar.

pool.q: Exposure to what risk factor is classically associated with ocular toxoplasmosis?

options.d: living in the Ohio River Valley

pool.rationale:
Ocular toxoplasmosis is caused by consumption of undercooked meat contaminated with cysts or oocytes of Toxoplasma gondii.
Expose to tick bites is a risk factor for tick-borne diseases, such as Lyme disease. Histoplasmosis, not toxoplasmosis, is endemic to the Ohio River Valley. Exposure to mosquitoes is associated with malaria.

pool.q: For a patient with age-related macular degeneration and initial, new-onset metamorphopsia, what is the most reasonable sequence of ancillary testing?

options.a: fundus photography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, fundus autofluorescence
options.b: spectral domain optical coherence tomography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, fluorescein angiography
options.c: spectral domain optical coherence tomography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, indocyanine green (ICG) angiography
options.d: fluorescein angiography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, spectral domain optical coherence tomography

pool.rationale:
Although controversy exists as to whether intravenous fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) is more sensitive in detecting exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FA may be necessary in this setting, as it may diagnose the retinal macroaneurysm, pseudophakic macular edema, branch retinal vein occlusion, and other confounders. However, there is no controversy about our goal to initially use the safest and least invasive diagnostic modality. Thus, the most reasonable sequence would be to do OCT before angiography in this setting. In straightforward cases, spectral domain OCT may be the only ancillary testing needed to initially diagnose a new case of exudative AMD. Once neovascularization is confirmed and/or other confounders excluded, OCT is very useful to noninvasively monitor response to therapy.
Fundus photography is excellent at documenting the macula examination on a particular day but does not provide additional diagnostic information like the other modalities listed. Autofluorescence is very useful in assessing the health of the RPE and the accumulation of lipofuscin but is not helpful in assessing initial metamorphopsia as OCT or even FA.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Laser photocoagulation is indicated for what complication of acquired retinal macroaneurysm?
pool.rationale: Focal laser photocoagulation is indicated for visually significant macular edema associated with acquired retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm. Dense vitreous hemorrhage and, less commonly, extensive subretinal hemorrhage, may be managed with vitrectomy surgery when clinically indicated. Retinal neovascularization is not a common complication of acquired retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presenting with a posterior vitreous detachment with pigment granules in the anterior vitreous (Shafer sign) is approximately how much more likely to have a retinal break than a patient without this presentation?
pool.rationale: Patients presenting with an acute posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) and pigment granules in the anterior vitreous, also known as a positive "Shafer sign" or "tobacco dust," are roughly 7 times more likely to have an associated retinal break than patients with PVD without pigment granules.

pool.q: Intravitreal bevacizumab has demonstrated efficacy in the management of diabetic macular edema and what other ophthalmic disorder?
pool.rationale: Anti–vascular epithelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) drugs, including bevacizumab, have been shown to be efficacious in treatment of choroidal neovascular membrane. Bevacizumab has no role in treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal effusion.

pool.q: What traumatic extraocular condition is associated with a branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO)?
pool.rationale:
A BRAO is the result of embolization or thrombosis of the affected vessel. Common sources of emboli include cholesterol emboli arising in the carotid arteries, platelet-fibrin emboli associated with large vessel arteriosclerosis, and calcific emboli arising from diseased cardiac valves.
Rare causes of a BRAO include emboli resulting from cardiac myxoma, fat emboli from long-bone fractures, septic emboli from infective endocarditis, and talc emboli from intravenous (IV) drug use.
Traumatic pancreatitis is associated with Purtscher retinopathy, which is associated with focal areas of retina whitening that may superficially resemble a BRAO, but is not a BRAO. Subarachnoid hemorrhage may be associated with intraocular hemorrhage or Terson syndrome.

pool.q: What two adhesion molecules attach the vitreous to the internal limiting membrane (ILM) of the retinal surface?
pool.rationale: The vitreous attaches to the internal limiting membrane (ILM) of the retinal surface primarily via fibronectin and laminin. The integrin molecule has been shown to induce posterior vitreous detachment, not facilitate attachment. The connectin molecule does not appear to play a significant role in vitreoretinal adhesion.

pool.q: What organism causes cat-scratch disease?
pool.rationale:
Bartonella henselae

Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae.
Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, which can result in irritation and inflammation of the eye and swelling of lymph glands near the ear. Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease.

pool.q: During evaluation of a patient with bilateral blurry vision of several weeks' duration, the ophthalmologist identifies bilateral macular edema with microaneurysms, neovascularization of the optic discs, and diffuse peripheral cotton wool spots and intraretinal hemorrhages. The patient reports a previous history of nasopharyngeal cancer. Blood glucose and HbA1C levels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
pool.rationale: In the setting of nasopharyngeal cancer, the diagnosis of radiation retinopathy is the most likely. Radiation retinopathy shares features of deep and superficial retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and microaneurysms, and retinal and/or optic nerve neovascularization, much like other microangiopathic retinal vascular disorders such as diabetic and sickle cell retinopathies. Typically, an exposure of at least 30-35 grays (Gy) of radiation is needed to develop signs of radiation retinopathy, although it may develop after as little as 15 Gy of external beam radiation. Findings usually manifest approximately 18 months following external beam radiation, although they may be present earlier, following plaque brachytherapy.

pool.q: What is the most common isolate from patients with filtering bleb-associated endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale:
Streptococcus species

Streptococcus species are the most common organisms isolated in bleb-associated endophthalmitis. This endophthalmitis may occur months to years following the primary operative procedure. Treatment is the same as for other forms of bacterial endophthalmitis. Given the greater virulence of Streptococcus species, the prognosis is more guarded. Staphylococcus species are less commonly the cause of this form of endophthalmitis. Candida albicans rarely is a causative organism, and herpes simplex is not a cause of bleb-associated endophthalmitis.

pool.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with decreased central vision. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan is performed and the image is shown below. What complication is most likely to occur?
pool.rationale:
The clinical presentation described is consistent with the vitreomacular traction syndrome (VMT), also known as vitreomacular adhesion (VMA). VMT is a disorder of the vitreoretinal interface, characterized by (a) an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), (b) an abnormally strong adherence of the posterior hyaloid face to the macula, and (c) anteroposterior traction exerted by the vitreous pulling at adherent sites on the macula, causing morphologic and possible visual symptoms. Focal attachment of the vitreous to the foveola can induce foveal cavitation and macular hole formation.
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can be caused by retinal breaks or tears that form during a posterior vitreous detachment. The scan shows VMT and an incomplete PVD, so this would be less likely.
VMT is not directly related to the development of choroidal neovascularization or peripheral retinoschisis.

pool.q: For a patient with initial onset of symptoms due to central serous choroidopathy, what is the preferred management?
pool.rationale: Central serous chorioretinopathy typically resolves spontaneously within weeks to months of onset. Persistent, symptomatic cases may respond to thermal laser photocoagulation and/or verteporfin photodynamic therapy. Systemic corticosteroid therapy may exacerbate the condition, as may systemic conditions associated with elevated serum cortisol levels.

pool.q: What vitreoretinal surgical technique is contraindicated in the management of tractional detachment in a patient with the retinal findings shown?
pool.rationale: The photo shown demonstrates "sea fan" neovascularization, a hallmark of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy. Placement of encircling scleral buckles has been associated with risk of anterior segment ischemia and/or necrosis in this patient population.

pool.q: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is under treatment with hydroxychloroquine. What factor places her at greatest risk of visual loss from toxicity?
pool.rationale: Because hydroxychloroquine is metabolized in the kidneys and liver, patients with renal insufficiency, such as those with lupus nephritis and diabetic nephropathy, are at increased risk for accumulation of toxic metabolites. Older patients are at greater risk than younger patients. The most recent data suggest that a hydroxychloroquine dosage of 5.0 mg/kg/day and a chloroquine dosage of 2.3 mg/kg/day based on the patient’s real body weight may be safer across all body mass indexes than the dosage recommendation of 6.5 mg/kg/day and 3 mg/kg/day, respectively using the patient’s ideal body weight. Glaucoma is not a risk factor. Other risk factors, not given as choices here, include higher dose and total dose of hydroxychloroquine.

pool.q: What peripheral retinal lesion is least likely to be associated with retinal tear or detachment?
pool.rationale: Paving-stone degeneration is not associated with increased retinal detachment risk because it does not affect the vitreoretinal interface, and histologically represents fusion or fibrosis of the retina with the choroid similar to laser or cryopexy treatment. It is important to distinguish between paving-stone degeneration and a localized spot of atrophy from a hole or tear associated with a cuff of subretinal fluid and subjacent retinal pigment epithelial atrophy.  Lattice degeneration is among the peripheral retinal lesions most associated with increased risk of retinal detachment. Meridional folds can develop a tear at the posterior edge of the fold, and zonular traction tufts are a cause of small retinal flap tears, often seen following cataract surgery.

pool.q: A 6-year-old boy presents for evaluation of decreased vision in his right eye, and is found to have a vitreous hemorrhage. His mother notes that there is a history of an eye condition on her side of the family. Fundus examination of the fellow eye, as well as the eyes of the patient's asymptomatic brother, identifies fine radial striae involving the maculae. What gene encodes the defective protein responsible for the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
RS1

In concert, vitreous hemorrhage, a male relative with fine radial folds in the maculae, and a maternal family history of eye disease are all suggestive of x-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). The gene involved in this condition is RS1, which encodes the adhesion protein retinoschisin, which is responsible for Müller cell integrity. Boys with congenital XLRS frequently present with vitreous hemorrhages from torn retinal vessels in areas of retinoschisis. Foveal schisis presents with small cystic spaces and fine radial striae in the central maculae, although patients may initially maintain very good central vision. Peripheral retinoschisis occurs in about 50% of cases, and the subsequent pigmentary change that may develop may be mistaken for retinitis pigmentosa.
PRPH2 is associated with multiple macular dystrophies, including adult-onset foveal vitelliform macular dystrophy, Stargardt disease, and the pattern dystrophies. ABCA4 is most commonly associated with Stargardt disease. RPE65 is associated with retinitis pigmentosa and a form of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA).

pool.q: What is the most common systemic adverse event associated with intravenous fluorescein angiography?
pool.rationale: Nausea is the most common systemic adverse event associated with intravenous fluorescein angiography, occurring in up to 5% of patients. Hives also occur in 5% of injections.  Hypotension is very rare. True thrombophlebitis is not associated with this procedure, although fluorescein extravasation at the injection site can result in pain, edema, and erythema, which is self-limiting and treated conservatively.

pool.q: In which retinal cells is the response measured in the pattern electroretinogram mainly generated?
pool.rationale: The pattern electroretinogram (PERG) shows the response of the central retina to a contrast stimulus. It is mostly generated by the retinal ganglion cells. The (full-field) ERG is not affected in patients with dysfunction confined to the macula. Patients with generalized retinal dysfunction, and thus with abnormal results on full-field ERGs, have an abnormal PERG only if the macula is involved.

pool.q: What cells are targeted by the cell-mediated immune response against cell antigens in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease?
pool.rationale: The cell-mediated immune response against cell antigens in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease is directed toward melanocytes. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease is a multisystemic disorder characterized by granulomatous panuveitis with exudative retinal detachment. It is often associated with neurologic and cutaneous manifestations. VKH disease occurs more commonly in patients with a genetic predisposition to the disease, including those from Asian, Middle Eastern, Hispanic, and Native American populations. Several human leukocyte antigen (HLA) associations have been found in patients with VKH disease, including HLA-DR4, HLA-DR53, and HLA-DQ4. Successful therapy for VKH disease is early and aggressive treatment with systemic corticosteroids, followed by local and/or steroid-sparing systemic therapy in selected patients.

pool.q: What imaging modality best helps determine the optimal time to surgically drain a suprachoroidal hemorrhage?
pool.rationale: When suprachoroidal hemorrhage occurs intraoperatively, immediate drainage is rarely effective, due to rapid coagulation of the blood. Waiting 7 to 14 days often allows the hemorrhage to liquefy. B-scan ultrasonography is useful to help identify clot liquefaction. B-scan ultrasonography is also useful to determine whether "kissing," or appositional, suprachoroidal hemorrhage is present and whether concurrent retinal detachment is present. In the presence of large suprachoroidal hemorrhage, there is often no view for OCT or FA. CT is not indicated to monitor suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

pool.q: In the context of ocular genetic disorders, what is the definition of pleiotropy?

options.a: Mutations in both alleles cause a disease phenotype.
options.b: Diverse phenotypes share mutations in a common causative gene.
options.c: Mutations in a single allele cause a disease phenotype.
options.d: Multiple genes give rise to the same phenotype.

pool.rationale: Pleiotropy is the term for mutations in a single gene that may lead to multiple phenotypes. An excellent example of this is the ABCA4 gene, which has differing phenotypes for different mutations within the gene. The most common phenotype caused by mutation of ABCA4 is Stargardt disease (autosomal recessive, requires both alleles to harbor disease-causing mutations), but other mutations may cause pattern dystrophy, cone–rod dystrophy, or autosomal-recessive retinitis pigmentosa. Genetic heterogeneity is the term that describes multiple genes that give rise to an indistinguishable phenotype. For instance, mutations in at least 17 different genes may lead to Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA). Disorders caused by a mutation in a single allele arise from dominant inheritance. If mutations in both alleles are necessary to cause disease, then the inheritance is recessive.

pool.q: A patient with no prior ophthalmic history had an uneventful cataract surgery 1 week ago but now complains of blurry vision and photophobia. The visual acuity is 20/400. A hypopyon and vitritis are present. What intervention is most appropriate?

options.a: tap and inject with anti-fungal drugs
options.c: immediate pars plana vitrectomy with capsulectomy and lens removal

pool.rationale: Acute-onset postoperative endophthalmitis occurs within 6 weeks of cataract surgery and has a bacterial etiology. In evaluating the final visual outcomes for patients with acute-onset endophthalmitis and an initial visual acuity better than light perception, the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS), which was completed in 1995, found no difference between the immediate vitrectomy group and the group treated by tap and inject with intravitreal antibiotics. Chronic or delayed-onset endophthalmitis occurs more than 6 weeks after surgery and can have a bacterial or fungal etiology. Definitive treatment of chronic endophthalmitis secondary to Propionibacterium acnes may require vitrectomy with total capsulectomy and removal or exchange of the intraocular lens.

pool.q: What surgical practice improves the prognosis for hole closure for a stage 3 full-thickness macular hole?

options.b: peeling of the inner limiting membrane
options.c: delaying surgery by several months after symptom onset

pool.rationale: Peeling of the inner limiting membrane (ILM), particularly in surgeries for stage 3 and 4 macular holes, has been demonstrated to improve the rate of hole closure. Peeling of the cortical vitreous is a common feature of vitrectomy for multiple macular diseases. Vitrectomy is advised for all recent macular holes that are stage 2 or higher: Although up to 50% of stage 1 holes may close spontaneously, prompt intervention is advised for stage 2 or higher holes, given an association between hole duration and outcome. Ocriplasmin is a recombinant protease administered by intravitreal injection and designed as an alternative to vitrectomy.

pool.q: In the modified Scheie classification of hypertensive retinopathy, what grade is defined by the presence of obvious narrowing with some focal irregularities and arteriovenous crossing changes?
pool.rationale:
Multiple systems for grading hypertensive retinopathy exist, including the modified Scheie classification, the Keith-Wagener-Barker classification, and the Wong-Mitchell classification. The Wong-Mitchell classification is a simplified version of the K-W-B system that considers the implications of retinal findings for systemic risk stratification.
The modified Scheie classification is in widespread use and is defined as:
Grade 0: No changes
Grade 1: Barely detectable arteriolar narrowing
Grade 2: More evident generalized narrowing with some focal constriction and arteriovenous crossing changes
Grade 3: Changes of Grades 1 and 2 with addition of hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots
Grade 4: Grade 3 changes plus optic disc edema

pool.q: A 54-year-old phakic myope presents with an acute symptomatic horseshoe tear in the right eye. What treatment is most appropriate?
pool.rationale: Acute symptomatic horseshoe tear warrants prompt laser retinopexy to surround the pathology and reduce likelihood of progression to retinal detachment. Observation carries risk of progression to retinal detachment that would be unsuitable for most clinical scenarios. Scleral buckling and pars plana vitrectomy are a surgical options for eyes with detached retina, and would not typically be the preferred choice for an uncomplicated retinal tear.

pool.q: In a patient with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), what characteristic abnormality, unique to this disease, can be seen on fluorescein angiography (FA)?
pool.rationale: FA imaging of an eye with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) may show fluorescein leakage in a pattern that resembles a smokestack. This pattern of fluorescein leakage is unique to CSC. Irregular window defects from RPE abnormalities are commonly seen, but similar-appearing changes can occur from other conditions, such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In some cases, the FA appears normal. Multifocal hyperfluorescence is not seen commonly in eyes with CSC. Lacy hyperfluorescence may be seen in rare instances, if the CSC is complicated by a choroidal neovascular membrane.

pool.q: A mutation of which gene in which cell type results in nonprogressive dysfunction in patients with nyctalopia and white dots?

options.a: RLBP1 gene mutation in retinal photoreceptors
options.b: RDH5 gene mutation in retinal photoreceptors
options.c: ABCA4 gene mutation in retinal pigmented epithelium
options.d: RDH5 gene mutation in retinal pigmented epithelium

pool.rationale:
RDH5 gene mutation in retinal pigmented epithelium

Fundus albipunctatus is caused by a mutation in the gene RDH5. RDH5 encodes 11-cis-retinol dehydrogenase, a microsomal enzyme in the RPE that converts 11-cis-retinol into 11-cis-retinal and is therefore involved in the regeneration of rhodopsin. Patients with mutations in this gene have very delayed rhodopsin regeneration, and although levels eventually normalize, the process can take many hours in the dark. Mutations in the gene RLBP1 result in retinitis punctata albescens. ABCA4 is a gene that, depending on the exact mutation, can cause Stargardt disease, fundus flavimaculatus, cone-rod dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and AMD, among others.

pool.q: What is the characteristic fundus appearance of dominant (familial) drusen?

options.a: clustering of lesions predominantly in the macula
options.b: drusen distribution beyond the temporal vascular arcades and nasal optic nerve margin
options.d: large soft drusen with irregular borders

pool.rationale:
A clinical feature characteristic for dominant (familial) drusen is the distribution of drusen beyond the temporal vascular arcades and nasal optic nerve margin. A single missense mutation (Arg345Trp) on exon 10 in the EFEMP1 gene of some patients with dominant drusen results in a fibrillin-like extracellular matrix protein expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina. The clinical findings typically first manifest bilaterally in the third to fourth decade of life. Although usually asymptomatic, choroidal neovascularization may develop in this patient population and lead to loss of vision.
In contrast to drusen of age-related macular degeneration (ARMD), the lesions of dominant drusen are typically small and round. Clumping and hyperplasia of the RPE and drusen clustering in the macula are features of ARMD, not familial drusen.
