pool.q: What is the most important step in minimizing the risk of endophthalmitis when performing an intravitreal injection?

options.a: using drugs from the same lot number when bilateral injections are performed
options.b: applying antibiotic eye drops after the injection
options.c: scrubbing the eyelid margin before the injection
options.d: applying povidone-iodine to the ocular surface before the injection

pool.rationale: The pre-procedure application of 5% povidone-iodine to the ocular surface is widely considered the most important step in preventing endophthalmitis following an intravitreal injection. The patient’s conjunctiva and eyelids are presumed to be the most common source of infection. Thus, while treatment of severe blepharitis is appropriate prior to initiating intravitreal injections, excessive manipulation of the lid margin immediately before an injection may increase the release of bacteria-contaminated secretions. The benefits of periprocedure topical antibiotics is controversial, and their use is not routinely recommended. Many practices employ a workflow in which medication from a different lot number is used for each eye when bilateral injections are performed to further minimize risk.

pool.q: What percentage of cones overall reside outside the foveal region?
pool.rationale: The density and distribution of photoreceptors vary with topographic location. In the fovea, cones are predominantly red- and green-sensitive, with a density exceeding 140,000 cones/mm2. The foveola has no rods. The fovea contains only photoreceptors, rods and cones, and processes of Müller cells. The number of cone photoreceptors decreases rapidly away from the fovea, even though 90% of cones overall reside outside the foveal region. The density of rods also decreases toward the periphery.

pool.q: What type of retinal detachment is associated with inflammation?
pool.rationale:
Exudative retinal detachments are caused by inflammatory conditions involving the eye.
Hypotony increases the risk of developing serous choroidal detachments and not exudative retinal detachment.
Horseshoe retinal tear can lead to a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
High myopia is associated with increased risk of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

pool.q: What is the etiology of Terson syndrome?
pool.rationale: Terson syndrome is the association of intraocular hemorrhage with acute intracranial hemorrhage. Hemorrhage may involve the subinternal limiting membrane potential space, the preretinal space, or the vitreous cavity.

pool.q: What organism is associated with severe posttraumatic endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale:
Bacillus

Bacillus cereus accounts for 25% cases of posttraumatic endophthalmitis, and it has a rapid and severe course that causes profound vision loss. It is associated with soil-contaminated injuries, especially those involving foreign bodies.
Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Candida are also causative organisms, although not necessarily in the posttraumatic setting.

pool.q: Infection with what causative organism of posttraumatic endophthalmitis results in the worst prognosis?
pool.rationale:
Bacillus cereus

Posttraumatic endophthalmitis due to Bacillus species infection has a dismal prognosis, owing to its rapid and severe course. Endophthalmitis develops after up to 7% of penetrating ocular injuries. Bacillus species, which rarely cause endophthalmitis in other settings, may account for up to 25% of posttraumatic endophthalmitis. E coli, Streptococcus spp, and Staphylococcus spp may lead to visual loss, but the course is typically not as aggressive as that for Bacillus spp.

pool.q: By what mode is the pictured disorder inherited?
pool.rationale:
The inheritance pattern of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP/Gardner syndrome) is autosomal dominant. Gardner syndrome, also known as familial colorectal polyposis, is characterized by the presence of multiple polyps in the colon, together with tumors outside the colon. The extracolonic tumors may include osteomas of the skull, thyroid cancer, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas, as well as the occurrence of desmoid tumors in approximately 15% of affected individuals.
The ocular hallmark of this disease is the presence of a pigmented fundus lesion similar to those found in congenital hypertrophy or hyperplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE). Singular lesions have little diagnostic significance and are not pathognomonic of FAP. The presence of 4 or more widely spaced, small lesions per eye and bilateral involvement suggest FAP. Lesions are often teardrop-shaped and average between 4 mm and 5 mm in size. They are usually located in the midperiphery of the fundus and exhibit autofluorescence on optical coherence tomography (OCT) testing. Atypical CHRPE is also associated with FAP.

pool.q: A patient complaining of recent blurring of the central vision has the retinal appearance shown in the image. What historical feature would suggest an explanatory diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Thioridazine retinal toxicity manifests as a bilateral granular macular pigmentary disturbance that can progress to a nummular atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris.
Solar maculopathy results in a subtle, localized, parafoveal pigmentary alteration.
Hydroxychloroquine toxicity presents as bulls-eye maculopathy.
Gyrate atrophy presents with circumscribed areas of peripheral atrophy of the RPE and choriocapillaris. Carriers will occasionally have localized or mild peripheral pigmentary granularity.

pool.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with sudden vision loss in the right eye. The visual acuity is hand motions right eye and 20/80 left eye. A vitreous hemorrhage is apparent in the right eye. Findings of the left fundus are shown in Figure 1. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
pool.rationale:
The clinical presentation is consistent with X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). The phenotype of congenital XLRS is variable, even within families. In pediatric patients, foveal schisis, which appears as small, cystoid spaces and fine radial striae in the central macula, can be best seen with optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence imaging. 

Central vision may initially be quite good and may remain stable for long periods, but it can eventually decline to 20/200 or worse. Peripheral retinoschisis may occur in up to 50% of patients. In severe cases involving peripheral schisis, there may be extensive areas of inner retinal elevation resembling total or subtotal retinal detachment. Histologic studies have shown that the splitting in peripheral XLRS occurs in the outer plexiform and nerve fiber layers. Boys with XLRS frequently present with vitreous hemorrhages from torn retinal vessels in areas of retinoschisis.

pool.q: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of macular hole formation?

options.b: reduced water transport of the retinal pigment epithelium
options.c: proliferation of glia, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), or hyalocytes at the vitreoretinal interface

pool.rationale: It has been hypothesized that a macular hole is caused by tangential traction as well as anterior posterior traction of the posterior hyaloid on the parafoveal region. It has not been shown that macular holes are related to reduced water transport of the retinal pigment epithelium. There is no acute loss of central photoreceptors when a macular hole develops. Proliferation of glia, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), or hyalocytes at the vitreoretinal interface, especially at the posterior pole, results in epiretinal membrane formation.

pool.q: For a pneumatic retinopexy to be effective, the retinal breaks should be confined to what clock-hours of the retina?
pool.rationale:
Classic indications for a pneumatic retinopexy are:
  • confidence that all retinal breaks have been identified
  • retinal breaks confined to the superior 8 clock-hours
  • a single or multiple retinal breaks within 1-2 clock-hours
  • the absence of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) grade CP or CA
  • clear media
  • patient who can maintain proper positioning

pool.q: Severe, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy may be defined by what feature?

options.c: at least 1 intraretinal hemorrhage in each of 4 quadrants
options.d: venous beading in at least 1 quadrant

pool.rationale: Severe, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy is associated with prominent intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in 1 or more quadrants. By definition, other findings include extensive (>20) intraretinal hemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants and venous beading in 2 or more quadrants. Vitreous hemorrhage is a finding in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

pool.q: What diagnostic item is used for the evaluation of contrast sensitivity?
pool.rationale: The Pelli-Robson test measures contrast sensitivity using a single, large letter size (20/60 optotype), with contrast varying across groups of letters. Patients read the letters, starting with the highest contrast and continue until they are unable to read 2 or 3 letters in a single group. The subject is assigned a score based on the contrast of the last group in which 2 or 3 letters were correctly read. The Pelli-Robson score is a logarithmic measure of the subject’s contrast sensitivity. The anomaloscope, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue test, and Ishihara plates are all used to evaluate color vision, not contrast sensitivity.

pool.q: What are typical features of acute retinal necrosis syndrome?

options.a: peripheral retinitis with circumferential spread, occlusive vasculitis, and vitritis
options.b: retinal whitening and edema with a macular cherry red spot
options.c: outer retinal necrosis, elevated intraocular pressure, marked absence of vitritis
options.d: prominent anterior chamber reaction with hypopyon, macular neuroretinitis, exudative retinal detachment

pool.rationale:
Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) typically presents as peripheral retinitis with circumferential spread, occlusive vasculitis, and vitritis. Retinal breaks develop in areas of necrosis, leading to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in many cases. ARN is typically associated with vitritis. Absence of vitritis is seen in progressive outer retinal necrosis in immunocompromised patients.
Prominent anterior chamber reaction with hypopyon, macular neuroretinitis, and exudative retinal detachment are not typically associated with acute retinal necrosis. Retinal whitening and edema with a macular cherry red spot is the typical description for a central retinal artery occlusion.

pool.q: In what form of dichromacy is the long-wavelength (L-cone) photopigment absent?

Such individuals lack one of the cone photopigments. About 2% of males have dichromacy; 1% are missing the long-wavelength (L-cone) photopigment, a disorder termed protanopia; and 1% are missing the medium-wavelength (M-cone) photopigment, called deuteranopia. A rare, third form of congenital dichromacy is lack of the short-wavelength (S-cone) photopigment, termed tritanopia, which is an autosomal-dominant defect that occurs in about 0.001% of the population.

pool.q: What systemic disorder is associated with asteroid hyalosis?
pool.rationale:
Asteroid hyalosis is associated with diabetes and hypertension.
Multiple myeloma, hypercholesterolemia, and hemochromatosis are not associated with asteroid hyalosis.

pool.q: A 7-year-old child with congenital sensorineural hearing loss has best corrected vision of 20/60 in each eye. What would the most likely examination finding be?
pool.rationale:
Usher syndrome, an association of retinitis pigmentosa and congenital sensorineural hearing loss, is suspected in this patient. There are 3 types of Usher syndrome and all have autosomal recessive inheritance:
  • Type 1: early and profound hearing loss, RP, vestibular areflexia
  • Type 2: born with moderate to severe hearing loss and develop RP within their second decade of life but have normal vestibular function
  • Type 3: progressive hearing loss, variable RP, and sporadic vestibular function
CHARGE syndrome (association of ocular coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, and genitourinary and ear anomalies) patients may have coloboma and hearing loss, but this is related to middle- and inner-ear abnormalities, and these patients may have unusually shaped external ears.
Anterior uveitis is not associated with congenital hearing loss.
Cataract is associated more commonly with other forms of retinitis pigmentosa.

pool.q: What premonitory symptom portends an impending central retinal artery occlusion?
pool.rationale:
Emboli within the carotid distribution that cause retinal artery occlusion can also cause amaurosis fugax or transient ischemic attacks.
Light sensitivity can be secondary to ocular surface diseases or uveitis. 
Flashes and floaters are associated with a symptomatic posterior vitreous detachment.
Central retinal artery occlusion is not associated with retro-orbital pain and is classically painless.

pool.q: A 40-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with an intracranial hemorrhage after a head injury. Dilated fundus examination shows vitreous and subhyaloid hemorrhage in both eyes. What is the likely long-term visual prognosis if baseline vision was normal and presuming the intracranial hemorrhage would resolve without any residual deficits?

options.c: Visual prognosis depends on timing of vitrectomy for vitreous/subhyaloid hemorrhage.
options.d: Visual function is usually unaffected once vitreous/subhyaloid hemorrhage clears.

Spontaneous improvement generally occurs, although vitrectomy is occasionally required to clear ocular media. Timing of vitrectomy has no bearing on final visual prognosis.

pool.q: One month ago, a 25-year-old woman experienced transient visual loss. Two days ago, she noted a "smudge" in the central vision of her right eye. Her visual acuity is 20/40 eccentrically OD and 20/20 OS. Her pupils react briskly without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Her left fundus is normal. Given that her right fundus is abnormal as shown, what finding might be expected?

options.c: scotoma on Amsler grid testing OD
options.d: inferior altitudinal visual field defect OD

pool.rationale: This patient has multiple retinal hemorrhages, disc edema, cotton-wool spots, and tortuous veins from a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). The absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect strongly suggests that this is a nonischemic CRVO. However, the reduction in visual acuity would likely be associated with macular edema, which would result in a central scotoma on Amsler grid testing. A superior branch retinal vein occlusion would be associated with an inferior altitudinal defect, but this finding would not be likely in a nonischemic CRVO. In CRVO, color vision should be relatively intact. Choroidal hypofluorescence would not be associated with a CRVO.

pool.q: A 20-year-old white man presents with 2 days of decreased vision in both eyes. He mentions that he enjoyed watching a solar eclipse 2 days ago. On examination, visual acuity is 20/60 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Both eyes show a yellow-white spot in the fovea. What characteristic finding on optical coherence tomography (OCT) will develop in the next several weeks?

options.a: subfoveal disruption, or loss, of layers of the inner retina
options.c: subfoveal disruption, or loss, of layers of the outer retina
options.d: disruption of the inner retinal architecture

pool.rationale: The patient presents with solar retinopathy. The condition is caused by direct or indirect viewing of the sun for a prolonged time period. Risk factors for developing solar retinopathy include using tetracycline or psoralens (found in PUVA, which is a treatment for eczema and psoriasis), and having clear lenses. The damage is due to shorter wavelengths with high energy, such as visible blue light and ultraviolet light. Examination reveals a white-yellow foveal dot that turns into a reddish dot several days later. After 2 weeks, an outer foveal defect may develop. Fluorescein angiography is typically normal in this disease. However, in the first 48 hours, a small focal area of staining may be seen.

pool.q: When evaluating a patient with vitreomacular traction syndrome for ocriplasmin injection, what ocular characteristic affects treatment prognosis?

pool.q: A patient with the fundus photograph and fluorescein angiogram shown is most likely to have what systemic disease?
pool.rationale: Acute central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is characterized by diffuse retinal whitening involving all quadrants, sclerotic retinal arterioles, and a cherry-red spot in the macula. An embolus in an arteriole may or may not be visible. CRAO is usually the result of atherosclerosis-related thrombosis and/or embolic cerebrovascular disease. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients presenting with CRAO.

pool.q: Of what material is asteroid hyalosis composed?
pool.rationale: The characteristic small, white, round vitreous opacities of asteroid hyalosis are composed of calcium-containing phospholipids. Calcium carbonate is typically found in bone or pathologic soft tissue calcification. Collagen I and cholesterol are not found in the vitreous (secondary vitreous contains largely collagen type II).

pool.q: How is "threshold disease" of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) defined?

options.a: 5 contiguous or 8 cumulative clock-hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation in zone II with any vascular engorgement
options.b: 3 contiguous or 10 cumulative clock-hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation in zone II with any vascular engorgement
options.c: 3 contiguous or 8 cumulative clock-hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation in zone III with any vascular engorgement
options.d: 6 clock-hours of any extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation in zone III with any vascular engorgement

pool.rationale: Initially proposed in the Cryotherapy for ROP Study and later in the Early Treatment ROP Study (ETROP), the threshold for conventional treatment is 5 contiguous or 8 cumulative clock-hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation (stage 3) in zone I or zone II with any vascular engorgement (plus disease).

pool.q: What finding is most typically associated with vitreoretinal tufts?
pool.rationale: Vitreoretinal tufts are small, peripheral focal areas of elevated glial tissue. They are typically found anterior to the equator and often nearer the ora serrata. They are rarely associated with retinal breaks, as they often occur anterior the posterior margin of the vitreous base.

pool.q: What treatment is recommended for a superotemporal meridional retinal fold without an associated retinal break?
pool.rationale: No treatment is required for a meridional retinal fold without an associated retinal break. Such folds represent redundant retina and are typically located in the superior nasal quadrant. They may be the site of a posterior vitreous separation-induced retinal tear, with or without a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Appropriate management of these complications is indicated in that instance.

pool.q: A 7-year-old girl with a recent history of blunt ocular trauma is found to have a circumferential linear break without retinal detachment along the ora serrata, and an avulsion of the vitreous base. What is the preferred management option?

options.d: pars plana vitrectomy with laser retinopexy

pool.rationale:
The vignette describes a traumatic dialysis without retinal detachment in a young patient. This is best treated with laser retinopexy, or cryopexy if the view is hazy, to reduce the risk of later retinal detachment.
Close observation is an option, since the development of retinal detachment after trauma in young patients occurs most often in a delayed fashion, due to vitreous liquefaction over the tear. Thirty percent (30%) of retinal detachments after trauma are identified within 1 month, 50% are identified within 8 months, and 80% are identified within 24 months.
Treatment with encircling scleral buckle and/or pars plana vitrectomy with laser retinopexy would be indicated if a retinal detachment develops.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist examines a patient who was previously diagnosed with ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. The presence of what posterior segment finding would suggest the diagnosis may be incorrect?
pool.rationale: Ocular histoplasmosis is characterized by "punched out" chorioretinal scars, juxtapapillary atrophic pigmentary changes, choroidal neovascularization (CNV), and the absence of vitritis. If vitritis is found in association with 1 or more elements of the classic triad of ocular histoplasmosis syndrome, then multifocal choroiditis or other uveitis should be considered as a diagnosis.

pool.q: In the absence of retinal or iris neovascularization, how would one categorize the severity of diabetic retinopathy illustrated?
pool.rationale: The image demonstrates severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). Venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) are both present and are characteristic of severe NPDR. This is not a characteristic of mild or moderate NPDR. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterized by the presence of retinal or iris neovascularization.

pool.q: What color (wavelengths) of light is readily absorbed by macular xanthophyll?
pool.rationale: Macular xanthophyll readily absorbs blue, but minimally absorbs yellow, red, and infrared wavelengths, so the blue wavelength should be avoided during laser photocoagulation, especially in the macula, to minimize thermal macular retinal damage.

pool.q: What is a cause of severe vision loss in patients with pathologic myopia?
pool.rationale: Choroidal neovascularization is a potential complication of degenerative myopia. Following early diagnosis, this complication may be effectively managed with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. Retinal neovascularization, retinal telangiectasis, and angioid streaks are not commonly associated with degenerative myopia.

pool.q: What type of identifiable cells can epiretinal membranes contain?
pool.rationale: Epiretinal membranes are composed of an extracellular matrix including collagen, as well as cells derived from glia (Müller cells, microglia, and fibrous astrocytes), retinal pigment epithelium, and immune cells. The cells differentiate over time into contractile myofibrocytes. These membranes are semi-translucent and avascular. They may be idiopathic, possibly related to vitreoretinal interface abnormalities after posterior vitreal detachment, possibly allowing glial cells to pass through the internal limiting membrane and reach the retinal surface, where they can propagate as a thin membrane. Epiretinal membranes may also be associated with other conditions including retinal vascular occlusions, trauma, and retinal tears, where retinal pigment epithelial cells, exposed to the vitreous, may migrate to the macular surface. The distortion induced by contraction of the membrane may lead to reduced acuity, or the development of a macular hole (figures). Soluble factors in the vitreous may play a role in stimulating the growth of epiretinal membranes and may also provoke their contraction, leading to surface wrinkling retinopathy, macular pucker, and macular holes.

pool.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive man presents with acute vision loss in the right eye. Examination reveals multifocal areas of deep retinal opacification, involving the retinal periphery in both eyes and the macula OD. What laboratory test would be useful in establishing the diagnosis?

options.a: CD4+ cell count, aqueous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus
options.b: purified protein derivative (PPD) test and chest x-ray
options.d: serum venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed (FTA-ABS) test

pool.rationale:
+ cell count, aqueous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus

The clinical description is suggestive of progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN), the etiology of which is the varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus. PORN occurs in immunocompromised patients, including those who are HIV positive, with a low CD4+ cell count. Although syphilis, tuberculosis, and/or a fungal infection can present with retinal involvement, multifocal retinitis of the depth and spatial distribution described above is characteristic of PORN.

pool.q: Within the retina, the density of rods is greatest at what degree of fixation?
pool.rationale: The rod photoreceptors have their greatest density (about 160,000 rods/mm2) within the retina at around 12 degrees of fixation. Rod density decreases toward the peripheral retina. Cone density is greatest (around 140,000 cones/mm2) in the fovea. Within the central fovea, only cones are observed. The fovea is defined as a concave central retinal depression seen on slit-lamp examination; it is approximately 1.5 mm in diameter.

pool.q: Aside from ingestion of cysts, by what route can ocular toxoplasmosis be transmitted?
pool.rationale: Toxoplasmosis may be transmitted by ingestion of tissue cysts or by hematogenous route, which includes transplacental fetal transmission. The obligatory intracellular parasites of toxoplasmosis may not be transmitted by saliva, fomite, or respiratory aerosolization.

pool.q: A 25-year-old man reports lifelong bilateral peripheral and night vision problems, and progressive vision loss. He has no family history of eye disorders. On dilated fundus examination, there is a pale optic nerve and attenuated vessels, as well as the finding shown in the figure below. When evaluating these retinal findings, what mimicking condition must the ophthalmologist also consider?
pool.rationale:
The figure shows dense peripheral bone spicules, a typical fundus finding in retinitis pigmentosa (RP). When evaluating suspected RP in a patient with a negative family history (simplex RP), the clinician must consider acquired causes of retinal degeneration that can mimic RP, including previous ophthalmic artery occlusion, diffuse uveitis, infections such as syphilis, paraneoplastic syndromes, and retinal drug toxicity. Secondary forms of pigmentary retinopathy associated with metabolic or other organ system disease must also be considered.
Toxoplasmosis would not give these fundus findings, which are characteristic for RP. A diagnosis of cone dystrophy is suggested by the progressive loss of visual acuity and color discrimination, often accompanied by hemeralopia (day blindness) and photophobia (light intolerance). Ophthalmoscopy may show a symmetric bull’s-eye pattern of macular atrophy or more severe atrophy, such as demarcated circular macular lesions. Previous trauma may cause retinal abnormalities, but would not present with progressive vision loss and night blindness.

pool.q: What layer of the retina is formed by Müller cell footplates?
pool.rationale:
The retina contains clinically relevant layers beyond its synaptic and cell body-containing layers that are identifiable by light microscopy and OCT. The ILM is formed by the footplates of Müller cells and is attached to the posterior cortical gel of the vitreous. The ILM is frequently removed during surgery for idiopathic macular holes (see Basic and Clinical Science Course, Section 12, Retina and Vitreous, Chapter 20, Vitreoretinal Surgery and Intravitreal Injections, for further discussion).
The ELM is a junctional complex, rather than a true membrane, that is formed by zonular attachments between Müller cells and photoreceptors. The MLM is located within the inner third of the outer plexiform layer and demarcates synaptic and structural associations between photoreceptors and bipolar cell processes. Like the ELM, the MLM is thus also a junctional structure, rather than a true membrane. Finally, the inner-outer segment junction (identified as the ellipsoid zone or EZ on OCT) demarcates the boundary between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptors and reflects the photoreceptor’s status as a modified ciliated cell. The integrity of the ELM and the EZ on OCT has implications for visual acuity.

pool.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with metamorphopsia in her right eye. Optical computed tomography (OCT) shows posterior hyaloid causing traction, with distortion of the foveal contour and cystic changes. The visual acuity is 20/80. What management approach is most likely to result in improved visual acuity?

options.d: pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with peeling of the internal limiting membrane

pool.rationale: Removal of traction with a pars plana vitrectomy has a very high rate of visual improvement. Spontaneous release of vitreomacular traction can occur but is less likely to lead to improvement in vision than PPV. Intravitreal ocriplasmin injection has been used to treat vitreomacular traction; however, its success rate is much lower than that of PPV. While triamcinolone can be used to treat many types of macular edema, it is less successful in treating edema caused by traction. Injection of t-PA is used to liquefy subretinal clotted blood and would not be beneficial in this patient.

pool.q: What electrophysiologic diagnostic study serves as a direct measure of macular function?
pool.rationale: The mfERG is useful in the diagnosis of macular dysfunction and in assessing the extent of central retinal involvement in generalized retinal disease by producing a topographic ERG map of the central retinal cone-system function. The stimulus consists of multiple hexagons, smaller in the center than the periphery, to reflect cone photoreceptor density, each of which flashes with a pseudorandom sequence. Cross-correlation techniques are used to calculate the small ERGs corresponding to each hexagon. Overall stimulus field size is approximately 50°. The EOG assesses the health of the RPE by measuring the changes in the corneo-retinal standing potential during light adaptation. The VEP, or VER, is a measurement of the electrical signal in the brain in response to light stimulus, recorded at the scalp over the occipital cortex; it is a measure of the integrity of the afferent visual pathway. The PERG is a measure of central RGC function and is a less-direct objective index of macular function than the mfERG.

pool.q: For the condition shown, what treatment has been proven to be effective for the associated macular edema?
pool.rationale:
The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRAVO) study found ranibizumab to be an effective treatment for macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Patients who got monthly injections of ranibizumab had better visual acuity gain than patients receiving sham injections at 6 months.
Verteporfin is used in photodynamic therapy and is not an approved treatment for macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Ocriplasmin is used for vitreomacular traction and has no role in treatment of macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Panretinal laser photocoagulation is not used for treating macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion.

pool.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman experienced blurred vision that did not resolve when her preeclampsia was treated. Six months after she delivered a healthy girl, she had normal visual acuity, scattered defects on automated perimetry, and patchy hyperpigmentation of both fundi. What is the most likely cause of her vision loss?
pool.rationale:

An amniotic fluid embolus could cause a branch or central retinal artery occlusion if it passed through a patent foramen ovale and could lead to altitudinal or diffuse visual field loss. Retinopathy of prematurity would not suddenly become symptomatic during pregnancy.

pool.q: What systemic disease is most commonly associated with endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis in North America?
pool.rationale:
Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis results from hematogenous seeding of the eye, typically during transient bacteremia. Although decreased vision and eye pain are common symptoms, many patients do not have any constitutional symptoms. A wide range of bacteria can cause endogenous  bacterial endophthalmitis. In North America, 40% of cases occur in patients with endocarditis, most typically caused by either Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species.
In contrast, 60% of endogenous endophthalmitis cases in Asia occur in patients with liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Nearly one-third of cases occur in patients who have urinary tract infections, most often caused by Escherichia coli. Other cases can be associated with intravenous drug use or with procedures known to produce bacteremia, particularly placement of indwelling catheters.
Clinical presentation can vary and depends on both the size of the inoculum and the virulence of the organism; it ranges from a focal chorioretinitis with little vitreous inflammation to a dense panophthalmitis that obscures the view of the posterior segment. The patient should undergo systemic evaluation for the source of infection and initiate treatment with systemic antibiotics. Additionally, intravitreal injection of broad-spectrum antibiotics should be considered.

pool.q: What is characteristic of retinal detachments following ocular blunt trauma in young eyes?

options.a: Retinal detachments in this setting have a delayed presentation.
options.b: Retinal detachments are almost always identified shortly after the trauma.
options.c: Retinal detachments in this setting typically progress rapidly.
options.d: Retinal detachments in this setting are typically bullous.

pool.rationale: Retinal detachments following trauma in young patients typically have a delayed presentation. The delay results from the fact that the vitreous is still formed (ie, not syneretic), which has 3 effects: the formed vitreous prevents fluid movement under the retina by acting like a cork on the break; the vitreous prevents the retina from assuming a bullous shape; the progression is slow as the vitreous slowly liquefies over time. Also, trauma in younger patients more often causes retinal dialyses rather than more typical retinal tearing at the posterior margin of the vitreous base. Retinal dialyses are notorious for delay between onset and retinal detachment.

pool.q: What is the cause of retinal ischemia in retinopathy of prematurity?
pool.rationale:
The absence of retinal vessels in the incompletely developed retinal periphery is the cause for retinal ischemia in retinopathy of prematurity. A decrease in retinal blood flow from oxygen-induced vasoconstriction may also contribute to the retinal ischemia.
Occlusion of formed retinal vessels and inflammation are not primary causes of the ischemia.
Neovascularization of the retina and vitreous are the result of ischemia, not its cause.

pool.q: What condition is a contraindication to B-scan echography?
pool.rationale:
Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, and magnetic intraocular foreign body are not contraindications for ocular ultrasonography.
However, if there is any suspicion for open ocular wounds (such as a large corneoscleral laceration), gonioscopy, scleral depression, and ultrasonography should all be avoided to prevent prolapse of intraocular structures.

pool.q: Intravitreal ganciclovir has been demonstrated to be efficacious for what ophthalmic disorder?
pool.rationale: Intravitreal ganciclovir, in addition to intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet, is used for treating cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Histoplasmosis usually does not require treatment unless choroidal neovascularization (CNV) develops in the macula. Toxoplasmosis is treated with triple therapy, and toxocariasis is managed with steroids.

pool.q: What ophthalmic diagnostic test is characteristically expected to give a normal result in patients with Best disease?
pool.rationale: An ERG is characteristically normal in Best disease. An EOG is typically abnormal, showing a severe loss of light response. OCT and FA results are abnormal in Best disease and reflect the changes in macular lesion from vitelliform stage to atrophic appearance.

pool.q: What characteristic of type 1 (exudative) juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasis differentiates it from type 2?
pool.rationale:
Type 1 juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia typically occurs unilaterally in young males and presents with aneurysmal dilation of the temporal macular vessels with cystoid macular edema and yellowish exudates. It is considered a variant of Coats disease and may respond to aflibercept, owing to the action of that anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agent on placental growth factor in addition to VEGF.

Progressive obliteration of perifoveal capillaries is seen in type 3 juxtafoveal telangiectasias.

pool.q: What distinguishes Purtscher retinopathy from Purtscherlike retinopathy?

options.a: a history of amniotic fluid embolism

pool.rationale:
Purtscher retinopathy was originally described after acute compression injuries to the chest or head resulting in vision loss in one or both eyes and accompanied by findings including peripapillary cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages, and retinal edema.
Purtscherlike retinopathy refers to overlapping fundus findings that, with the exception of fat emboli from long-bone fractures, result from nontraumatic etiologies. Amniotic fluid embolism, acute pancreatitis, and retrobulbar anesthesia are all associated with Purtscherlike retinopathy. The shared mechanism of Purtscher and Purtscherlike retinopathy is thought to be injury-induced complement activation that causes granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization that then occlude small arterioles such as those in the peripapillary retina.

pool.q: What management is recommended for this peripheral retinal lesion for a patient with asymptomatic high myopia?
pool.rationale: Vitreoretinal tufts without an associated retinal break can be safely observed in an asymptomatic patient. Laser retinopexy or cryopexy may be indicated in patients with retinal break associated with vitreoretinal tuft. Scleral buckle surgery may be indicated if a retinal break leads to a retinal detachment.

pool.q: What is a risk factor for epiretinal membrane (ERM) formation?
pool.rationale: Detachment or separation of the posterior vitreous is present in almost all eyes with idiopathic epiretinal membranes, and may be a requisite for ERM development. It is the result of proliferating glia, retinal pigment epithelial cells, and/or hyalocytes on the macular surface following PVD. ERM formation is not associated with chronic hydroxychloroquine use, degenerative retinoschisis, or LASIK.

pool.q: A patient incurs an acute compression injury to the thorax and experiences sudden loss of vision in both eyes. Each eye exhibits large retinal white spots, hemorrhages, and retinal edema. What factor would explain the relationship between the compression injury and the retinal findings?

options.a: acute rise in systolic blood pressure
options.c: compression of the central retinal vein
options.d: acute rise in intraocular venous pressure

pool.rationale: Purtscher retinopathy typically follows acute compression injuries to the thorax or head. It is thought to be a result of injury-induced complement activation, which causes granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization. This process in turn occludes small arterioles such as those found in the peripapillary retina.

pool.q: What retinal defect is most likely to be associated with traumatic injury?
pool.rationale: A retinal dialysis is the most common retinal defect associated with a traumatic injury. Horseshoe retinal tears and operculated retinal breaks can result from blunt trauma; however, they typically result from spontaneous posterior vitreous separation. Atrophic retinal holes are most commonly associated with lattice degeneration.

pool.q: According to the definition of the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS; Clinical Trial 20-1), acute postoperative endophthalmitis may develop during what interval following cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: Based upon the entry criteria for the EVS, the selected duration of acute postoperative endophthalmitis was 6 weeks. This interval was chosen to distinguish likely bacterial causes from potential fungal or other causes. The recommendation of the EVS—that patients with vision of hand motions (HM) or better who were treated with anterior chamber and vitreous aspiration and vitreous antibiotic injection had outcomes similar to those of patients managed with vitrectomy, anterior chamber and vitreous sampling, and vitreous antibiotic injection—applies only to patients who met the study entry criteria; that is, only those who presented with endophthalmitis in the initial postoperative 6-week interval.

pool.q: What clinical feature is most likely to occur after retinopathy of prematurity has been treated?

options.b: ridge at the edge of the vascularized retina

pool.rationale: Acute, rather than chronic, retinopathy of prematurity is characterized by retinal neovascularization and/or antecedent tissue ("ridge"), and dilated or engorged posterior veins ("plus disease"). Myopia, especially high myopia, is a characteristic often observed in treated retinopathy of prematurity.

pool.q: What is the inheritance pattern of choroideremia?
pool.rationale: The inheritance pattern of choroideremia is X-linked recessive. The disease is caused by mutations in the CHM gene, which is located at Xq21.2 and encodes for a geranylgeranyl transferase Rab escort protein. It is characterized by diffuse and progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. In affected males, the degeneration initially manifests as mottled areas of pigmentation in the anterior equatorial region and macula. The anterior areas gradually degenerate to confluent scalloped areas of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. Patients have night blindness and show progressive peripheral visual field loss over 3 to 5 decades. Most patients maintain good visual acuity.

pool.q: What is the preferred management for nonexudative angioid streaks?
pool.rationale: Safety glasses are an advisable precaution for patients with angioid streaks, who can be highly susceptible to choroidal rupture following even minor blunt injury. Vitrectomy, dietary supplements, and oral prednisone have no place in managing angioid streaks, especially in the absence of choroidal neovascularization.

pool.q: A male patient presents with photophobia, iris transillumination, hypopigmented fundi, and nystagmus. He has normal pigmentation of skin and hair. What inheritance pattern is most likely in this patient?
pool.rationale: Albinism includes a group of different genetic abnormalities in which the synthesis of melanin is reduced or absent. A number of genes are associated with both oculocutaneous and ocular albinism. Oculocutaneous albinism is typically transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Ocular albinism is typically transmitted as an X-linked (recessive) trait.

pool.q: In an asymptomatic patient with diabetes mellitus, what is the most important initial diagnostic evaluation to determine the presence of diabetic retinopathy?
pool.rationale:
Several level 1, randomized, controlled studies demonstrate the ability of timely treatment to reduce the rate and severity of vision loss from diabetes (eg, Diabetic Retinopathy Study, Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study). Examination prerequisites to applying the study results are accurate documentation of the presence and severity of peripheral diabetic retinopathy and macular edema. Although the other diagnostic procedures listed are useful in the evaluation of diabetic retinopathy, a dilated macular or fundus examination is a prerequisite to determine the presence and severity of disease.
In the RAND chronic disease quality project, while administrative data indicated that roughly half of the patients had an eye examination in the recommended time period, chart review data indicated that only 19% had documented evidence of a dilated examination. Thus, ensuring timely treatment that could prevent 95% of the blindness due to diabetes requires the performance and documentation of key examination parameters. The documented level of severity of retinopathy and the documented presence or absence of macular edema assists with the ongoing plan of care for the patient with diabetic retinopathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), what is an indication to initiate Age-Related Eye Disease Study [AREDS] vitamin therapy?
pool.rationale: In the original AREDS and in AREDS2, participants who benefited from antioxidant vitamin and mineral supplementation were those who had either intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in 1 eye. For participants with extensive intermediate (ie, medium-sized) drusen in 1 or both eyes, 1 or more large drusen in at least 1 eye, nonsubfoveal geographic atrophy in 1 eye, or advanced AMD (ie, subfoveal geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization [CNV]) in 1 eye who had been assigned to the group using the combination treatment of antioxidant vitamins with zinc and copper, the rate of development of advanced AMD at 5 years was reduced by 25%. The risk of losing vision of 3 or more lines (moderate vision loss) was reduced by 19% with this combination treatment.

pool.q: A 40-year-old patient initially demonstrates the findings shown in the first figure. Later the patient develops a choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) and a disciform scar.  A mutation of what gene should be suspected?
pool.rationale:
TIMP3

When early-onset drusen are associated with CNV in young adulthood, the diagnosis of Sorsby macular dystrophy should be considered. The diagnosis can be confirmed by demonstrating a disease-causing mutation in the TIMP3 gene. Doyne honeycomb dystrophy, Malattia Leventinese, and radial drusen are the same disorder, and are caused by a mutation in the EFEMP1 gene. Cuticular drusen is a clinical syndrome of small clustered drusen in young adults. Although associated with mutation in complement factor H, in contrast to the other choices, cuticular drusen is not a monogenic disorder.
Mutations in NYX are associated with congenital stationary night blindness.

pool.q: A 75-year-old woman with nonexudative age-related macular degeneration complains of increasing difficulty reading the newspaper since her last visit 6 months earlier. Her visual acuity, examination, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) results are stable. What test results might provide a correlate to her symptom?
pool.rationale: Compromised contrast sensitivity can be a major functional impediment that is disproportionate to visual acuity. Traditional newsprint is a relatively low-contrast target, particularly in comparison to the high-contrast Snellen chart. The Pelli-Robson test of contrast sensitivity might produce a score indicating abnormal contrast sensitivity in this patient. Although classically used to assess night blindness (nyctalopia), dark adaptometry can also reveal abnormalities in individuals with age-related macular degeneration. These deficits, however, are less likely to be related to the patient’s current task-specific complaint. Similarly, photostress recovery time can be abnormal in patients with age-related macular degeneration, but it would be less likely to correspond to the present complaint. The Farnsworth Panel D-15 test provides a quick method of assessing color deficiency.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complications of retinal cavernous hemangiomas require treatment?
pool.rationale:
Retinal cavernous hemangiomas may bleed into the vitreous in rare instances. Treatment of retinal cavernous hemangiomas is indicated in cases with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage. Laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy may be used. Lipid exudation and retinal neovascularization do not typically occur from retinal cavernous hemangiomas. The lesions are static, so progressive enlargement is not expected or seen.
In contrast, retinal hemangioblastomas associated with von Hippel–Lindau syndrome can result in visually significant lipid exudation requiring treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging test is most appropriate in the initial evaluation of ocular trauma?

options.b: computed tomography (CT) of the eye and orbit

pool.rationale: All the listed tests are helpful in evaluating ocular trauma, particularly to assess for the presence or absence of an intraocular foreign body. Plain films, although still useful, might not allow visualization of small metallic or nonradiopaque foreign bodies. Ocular ultrasonography must be performed with great caution, particularly when the eye is open, as compression of the eye can lead to extrusion of intraocular content. MRI can be performed only after the presence of a ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body has been excluded and should therefore be avoided in the initial assessment. MRI offers the advantage of providing visualization of even nonradiopaque material such as wood. While a CT scan of the orbits might not allow visualization of nonradiopaque foreign bodies, it is safe to perform and should be the first choice for imaging in most cases.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Enclosed ora bays may be associated with what potential complication?
pool.rationale: Enclosed oral bays may be associated with retinal tears and detachment, but are not associated with lens colobomas, retinal neovascularization, or malignant transformation.

pool.q: A 23-year-old man presents with poor night vision and peripheral vision loss for several years. Fundus examination is shown in the image below. The patient's mother is unaffected by the disease, and he is unaware of his father's medical history because his mother remarried shortly after he was born. What mode of inheritance is responsible for the patient's condition?

options.a: Genetic testing must be done to correctly determine the mode of inheritance of this disease.
options.b: The mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant and the affected allele was likely passed on by the father.
options.c: The mode of inheritance of this disease is X-linked recessive and the affected allele was passed on by the mother.
options.d: The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive and affected alleles were passed on by both parents.

pool.rationale: The clinical vignette and image demonstrate a case of rod-cone dystrophy or retinitis pigmentosa. Fundus findings may show waxy pallor of the optic nerve, arteriolar narrowing, and variable amounts of bone spicule-like changes in the periphery. The mode of inheritance is variable, with multiple mutations leading to this disease.

pool.q: Under what circumstances is visual acuity of 20/40 or better most likely to be preserved after central retinal artery occlusion?

options.a: when the fovea is supplied by a cilioretinal artery
options.b: when acute ophthalmic artery occlusion is determined to be the final diagnosis
options.c: when paracentesis is performed within 2 hours after onset of vision loss
options.d: when the papillomacular bundle is supplied by a patent cilioretinal artery

pool.rationale: In the setting of a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), a patent cilioretinal artery that supplies the fovea specifically, rather than the papillomacular bundle in general, can spare the central macular function and allow for preservation of visual acuity of 20/40 or better. Cilioretinal arteries occur in approximately 18% to 32% of eyes and contribute to the macular circulation of approximately 15% of eyes. Anterior chamber paracentesis has not predictably been proven to improve the visual outcome in CRAO. Acute ophthalmic artery occlusion is rare and has a generally poor visual prognosis.

pool.q: A 40-year-old woman with a remote history of intravenous (IV) drug use is incidentally found to have bilateral macular crystals. She denies any visual symptoms and has normal visual acuity. The fundus examination shows small crystalline particles in a vascular distribution throughout each macula. What complication can be associated with these findings?
pool.rationale: The history and fundus findings suggest talc emboli related to the history of IV drug use. The refractile talc particles, which have an intravascular location, do not typically cause vision loss. Instead, the most likely complication is peripheral neovascularization. Cystoid macular edema and central vision loss are features of tamoxifen retinopathy. Macular telangiectasia, which can also be accompanied by intraretinal crystals and result in central vision loss, can be complicated by subretinal neovascularization.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What metabolic disorder is most likely to result in a cherry red spot?
pool.rationale: The most common cause of a cherry-red spot from metabolic disorder is Tay-Sachs disease. Other metabolic syndromes, such as Niemann-Pick disease, can also cause cherry-red spots. Hunter and Hurler syndromes cause a pigmentary retinopathy, whereas Gaucher disease causes white preretinal opacities that are well visualized with OCT imaging.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a classic indication for pneumatic retinopexy?

options.a: absence of proliferative vitreoretinopathy grade A or B
options.c: ability to view entire retinal periphery

pool.rationale: The classic indications for pneumatic retinopexy include confidence that all retinal breaks have been identified, retinal breaks that are confined to the superior 8 clock-hours, a single retinal break, multiple breaks within 1–2 clock-hours, the absence of proliferative vitreoretinopathy grade CP or CA, a cooperative patient who can maintain proper positioning, and clear media.

pool.q: On examination with scleral depression, what characteristics of a retinal detachment are most consistent with a tractional retinal detachment?

options.b: mobile retina and retinal elevation changes with position
options.c: immobile retina and concave retinal elevation that does not usually extend to the ora serrata
options.d: mobile retina and convex retinal elevation that usually extends to ora serrata

pool.rationale:
Tractional retinal detachment has a smooth, concave retinal surface that is immobile, and the detachment usually does not extend to the ora serrata.
Mobile retina with retinal breaks and convex elevation that extends to ora serrata is seen in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
Retinal elevation that shifts with change in position is consistent with exudative retinal detachment.

pool.q: What is a characteristic clinical feature of hypertensive choroidopathy?
pool.rationale:
Elschnig spots are a common characteristic clinical feature of hypertensive choroidopathy. They manifest as black spots surrounded by bright yellow or red halos. Elschnig spots are caused by acute hypertensive events of the choroidal vascular system, mostly in the young. These changes in blood pressure cause an infarct of the vessels, leading to atrophy of the RPE and photoreceptors they support, creating tan patches that, in time, become hyperpigmented and surrounded by margins of hypopigmentation.
Retinal hemorrhages, exudates and optic disc edema are found in hypertensive retinopathy and hypertensive optic neuropathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For patients with clinically significant cataracts and diabetic macular edema (DME), what should preoperative management include?

options.a: Advise the patient to avoid surgery because disease progression is inevitable.
options.c: Plan to use a small capsulorrhexis to avoid development of rubeosis.
options.d: Consider pretreating the patient with an anti-VEGF agent.

pool.rationale: It is advisable to treat any pre-existing DME prior to cataract surgery to minimize or prevent worsening as a result of the surgical procedure. In patients with DME, anti-VEGF agents are excellent treatment options and can help reduce the risk of worsening the macular edema. Progression of diabetic retinopathy or DME is not inevitable if managed appropriately and aggressively. PRP sometimes worsens DME in the short run, but might help reduce it in the long run. A small capsulorrhexis would have no expected impact in preventing worsening of DME.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One week after cataract extraction, a 55-year-old man presents with ocular pain, visual acuity of light perception without projection, severe anterior chamber inflammation, and vitreous opacification. Acute postoperative endophthalmitis is suspected. What management approach is most appropriate?

options.a: immediate vitreous tap, await culture results prior to intravitreal antibiotic injection
options.b: immediate vitrectomy and empiric intravitreal antibiotic injection
options.c: immediate vitreous tap and empiric intravitreal antibiotic injection
options.d: immediate vitrectomy, await culture results prior to intravitreal antibiotic injection

pool.rationale: The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) evaluated the role of empiric intravitreal antibiotic therapy following either immediate vitrectomy or immediate diagnostic vitreous tap in the management of acute postoperative endophthalmitis. There was no statistically significant visual acuity outcome difference in the 2 groups if the vision at presentation was hand motions or better. There was a difference in outcome favoring the vitrectomy group when the presenting vision was light perception.

pool.q: What complication of fluorescein angiography is most common?
pool.rationale: Orange discoloration of the urine occurs in all patients. The most common adverse effects include nausea and vomiting (in approximately 5% of injections) and hives (in 5%). Most serious side effects such as hypotension, shock, laryngospasm, or even death have occurred in rare cases.

pool.q: What is a risk factor for idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy  (CSC)?
pool.rationale: Exogenous intake of corticosteroids, such as oral prednisone, is a risk factor for CSC. There is no known association between CSC and obesity or hydroxychloroquine use. CSC is more common in males, although there is an association between CSC and pregnancy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 57-year-old man presents with central visual distortion and findings consistent with a stage 1 macular hole. What is the best management option?

options.a: pars plana vitrectomy, removal of the posterior hyaloid, gas tamponade, and face-down positioning
options.b: pars plana vitrectomy, removal of both the posterior hyaloid and the internal limiting membrane (ILM), gas tamponade, and face-down positioning
options.c: pars plana vitrectomy, removal of both the posterior hyaloid and the internal limiting membrane, silicone oil tamponade, and no face-down positioning

pool.rationale: A stage 1 idiopathic macular hole is a premacular hole lesion with a 50% probability of spontaneous regression. Observation is the treatment of choice. If the lesion progresses to a full-thickness hole (stage 2, 3, or 4), then vitrectomy with posterior hyaloid peeling with or without ILM peeling and gas or silicone oil would be indicated.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An eye with high myopia has a posterior staphyloma and a macular detachment that does not extend beyond the vascular arcades. The peripheral retina is attached without any breaks. What is the most likely associated macular finding?
pool.rationale:
A macular hole in an eye with high myopia and posterior staphyloma can lead to a rhegmatogenous macular detachment.
Optic pit maculopathy can lead to a macular detachment in the setting of an optic pit. It is not associated with high myopia and posterior staphyloma, however.
Lacquer cracks and subretinal hemorrhage can be seen in high myopia, but they are not associated with macular detachment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging modality is best at delineating vitreomacular traction (VMT)?
pool.rationale: OCT is the most useful diagnostic study for the evaluation of suspected VMT, as demonstrated in the figure. The spacial resolution of OCT exceeds that of currently available B-scan ultrasonography. Fluorescein angiography may demonstrate cystoid macular edema associated with VMT but does not directly demonstrate the anatomic characteristics of VMT. Fundus photography has low specificity and selectivity for the detection of VMT.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What initial treatment would be preferred in the management of macular edema associated with central retinal venous occlusion?
pool.rationale: Intermittent intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy has been shown to temporarily reduce the macular edema and in most cases improve the visual acuity due to macular edema that is associated with central retinal venous occlusion (CRVO). Macular grid laser photocoagulation has not demonstrated proven efficacy in this condition. This question was addressed by the Central Retinal Vein Occlusion Study, which did not find that focal laser photocoagulation was of benefit in this setting. Panretinal photocoagulation is indicated for neovascularization associated with CRVO. Pars plana vitrectomy is indicated in the management of vitreous hemorrhage complicating CRVO.

pool.q: Stage 3 macular hole is characterized by what clinical feature?

options.b: full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina with a complete posterior vitreous detachment
options.c: full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina <400 µm in diameter
options.d: full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina >=400 µm in diameter

pool.rationale:
Stage 3 macular hole is characterized by full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina ≥400 μm in diameter.
Stage 2 macular hole is a full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina <400 μm in diameter.
Full-thickness defect in the neurosensory retina with a complete posterior vitreous detachment represents a stage 4 macular hole.
Foveal yellow ring is seen in a stage 1 (impending) macular hole.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most important management step in a patient who presents with a branch retinal artery occlusion?

options.a: checking erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and platelets

pool.rationale: Branch retinal artery occlusions are considered embolic events. Retinal arterial emboli have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality; therefore, emergent referral for embolic workup that includes brain imaging, evaluation of carotid arteries, and transesophageal echocardiography should be considered. Checking erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and platelets would be relevant if giant cell arteritis is suspected, but that would be less likely with a branch retinal artery occlusion. Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) and applying intermittent pressure on the globe (“ocular massage”) have been suggested but have not been found to be consistently effective in improving the patient’s visual prognosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Retina & Vitreous — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What identifiable preoperative feature increases the risk of ocular perforation during injection of retrobulbar anesthesia?

options.a: use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) at night

pool.rationale: Axial high myopia is a risk factor for ocular perforation with a retrobulbar injection. It is a relative, not an absolute, contraindication. Older age is not a contraindication to retrobulbar anesthesia injection. Use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is a relative contraindication to general anesthesia, not retrobulbar anesthesia, because laryngeal swelling following intubation may necessitate hospitalization for postanesthesia observation. Because obesity may make endotracheal intubation more difficult, the use of retrobulbar anesthesia would be favored.

pool.q: A 47-year-old woman developed the sudden onset of severe headache and "spots" in both eyes. She had a head computed tomography (CT) scan without contrast that is read as normal. She is treated with pain medication, and the headache improves but persists for 2 more days. On examination, her visual acuity is 20/25 OU, her pupils react briskly without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and her color vision, confrontation visual fields, and anterior segment slit-lamp examination are normal. The ophthalmologist notices a few cells in the vitreous and observes the fundus shown in the figures. What test is recommended next for this patient?

options.b: orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fat suppression and contrast

pool.rationale:
The presence of superficial and deep retinal hemorrhages in the setting of an acute-onset headache suggest the possibility of malignant hypertension and Terson syndrome, which is the association of intracranial hemorrhage (usually subarachnoid) with intraocular hemorrhage. If this patient had malignant hypertension, then the clinician would also expect to see disc edema, which is absent. Subarachnoid hemorrhage may not be detected by CT scan in 10% of patients; therefore, a lumbar puncture may be necessary to diagnose her.
Carotid ultrasonography is useful when evaluating carotid obstruction, retinal artery occlusion, or ocular ischemic syndrome, none of which is present here. A vitreous tap or aspirate would show red blood cells in the vitreous, but this is already known. An orbital MRI might reveal nerve sheath hemorrhages, but it is usually normal in Terson syndrome.

pool.q: A stage 3 macular hole is full thickness and at least what diameter (μm)?
pool.rationale: Stage 0 (premacular) holes represent vitreomacular adhesion (VMA). Stage 1A holes demonstrate foveal pseudocysts with foveal traction, 1B holes represent outer breaks in the fovea. Stage 2 holes are early full-thickness holes less than 400 μm in diameter. Stage 3 holes are full-thickness holes at least 400 μm in diameter, and stage 4 holes are full-thickness holes at least 400 μm in diameter in association with a complete posterior vitreous detachment.

pool.q: What management has been proven to be effective in reducing the risk of vision loss from intermediate, nonexudative age-related macular degeneration?
pool.rationale: The Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) demonstrated that taking beta-carotene, vitamin E and C, and zinc reduce the rate of visual loss to advanced age-related macular degeneration (AMD) for patients with intermediate or advanced AMD in one eye. The other treatments have not been proven to be effective in randomized clinical trials, although all of the alternatives have been suggested as beneficial based upon epidemiological studies. Surveys have demonstrated that there is a significant barrier to translating the AREDS study findings, and reports have noted that up to 50% of applicable patients do not have AREDS supplements prescribed or recommended.

pool.q: What agent used for retinal tamponade persists in the eye for approximately 2 months after a pars plana vitrectomy?
pool.rationale: Perfluoropropane gas (C3F8) lasts for approximately 2 months in the eye after a vitrectomy and thus provides a longer-lasting tamponade than sulfur hexafluoride gas (SF6), which lasts for 2 to 3 weeks. Perfluorocarbon liquids such as perfluoro-n-octane (PFO), which are heavier than water, can be used for temporary intraoperative stabilization of the retina, but they are not left in the eye. Silicone oil must be surgically removed.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is preparing to treat a 72-year-old patient for choroidal neovascularization with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy in the right eye. The left eye has confluent drusen. What would be appropriate to explain to the patient regarding the left eye?

options.a: Anti-VEGF injections are needed for left eye as well.
options.b: Risk of choroidal neovascularization in left eye is very low.
options.c: The use of daily Amsler grid testing is needed.
options.d: Photodynamic therapy is needed for left eye.

pool.rationale:
The fellow eye of an individual with unilateral neovascular age-related macular degeneration is at high risk for developing choroidal neovascularization. These patients should be instructed on daily Amsler grid monitoring. Give yourself full points if you answered "Use of AREDS vitamins is recommended" in challenge mode.
Anti-VEGF injections and photodynamic therapy are used to treat neovascular maculopathy; they have no role in treating an eye with confluent drusen without choroidal neovascularization.

pool.q: What is the most likely diagnosis for the fundus shown?
pool.rationale: This patient has neovascularization of the disc with nasal fibrous proliferation along the vascular arcades. Although other conditions, such as a venous occlusion, posterior uveitis, inherited peripheral retinal ischemia (eg, Norrie disease, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, and incontinentia pigmenti), may lead to this complication, proliferative diabetic retinopathy is by far the most likely and is supported by the other retinal abnormalities present, such as preretinal hemorrhage, intraretinal hemorrhage, and macular exudate. Although sickle cell retinopathy can cause neovascularization, findings are more likely in the peripheral retina.

pool.q: A patient reports lifelong poor night vision. The fundus examination shows numerous yellow-white dots, sparing the fovea but scattered throughout the posterior pole and mid-periphery. An initial electroretinogram (ERG) shows undetectable rod signals after a standard 30 minutes of dark adaptation, but the signals normalize in 1 eye that undergoes overnight dark adaptation. What is the diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Normalization of rod ERG responses with prolonged dark adaptation distinguishes the stationary condition fundus albipunctatus from retinitis punctata albescens. Both conditions are characterized by numerous retinal flecks, but retinitis punctata albescens is a progressive rod-cone dystrophy in which prolonged dark adaptation does not result in a full rescue of rod signals on ERG. Bone spicules may sometimes be absent in retinitis pigmentosa (RP sine pigmento), but the atrophic appearance of the peripheral retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) still differs from the discrete retinal flecks of either fundus albipunctatus or retinitis punctata albescens. As with the latter diagnosis, the ERG in RP does not normalize with dark adaptation. Fundus flavimaculatus describes a Stargardt disease phenotype in which subretinal flecks are widely scattered throughout the fundus.

pool.q: When administered as an intravitreal injection for retinal vascular disease, what drug is most likely to cause prolonged ocular hypertension or glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Triamcinolone acetonide, a corticosteroid, is the most likely medication of those listed to cause a prolonged increase in intraocular pressure when administered intravitreally. The other 3 medications listed (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept) are anti-vascular endothelial growth (anti-VEGF) agents, which, as a class, are much less likely to demonstrate this effect.

pool.q: A 62-year-old female presents with recent-onset flashing lights and a large, ring-shaped floater in her vision. The ophthalmologist promptly diagnoses a posterior vitreous detachment. At the slit lamp, pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous are evident. A fundus examination using a binocular indirect ophthalmoscope and scleral depression is performed. Where is a retinal tear most likely to be found?

options.a: anterior edge of the vitreous base
options.b: posterior edge of the vitreous base

pool.rationale: The vitreous is most firmly attached at the vitreous base, the optic disc margin, major blood vessels, edges of lattice degeneration, and chorioretinal scars. After a posterior vitreous detachment, the vitreous remains attached to the retina at the vitreous base, and traction on the retina can produce a tear. The most common site of retinal tears is the posterior margin of the vitreous base.

pool.q: What is the most likely mechanism for vitreous hemorrhage associated with laser photocoagulation?

options.a: small-diameter, high-intensity burns can perforate blood vessels
options.b: small spot size and short duration can rupture Bruch membrane
options.c: photocoagulation may precipitate tears of the pigment epithelium
options.d: extensive, intense photocoagulation can lead to massive chorioretinal edema

pool.rationale:
Focal treatment with small-diameter, high-intensity burns may cause vascular occlusion or perforate blood vessels, leading to preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage.
Small spot size, high power, and short duration of applications all increase the risk of a rupture in Bruch membrane, which may give rise to hemorrhage from the choriocapillaris and development of choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
Extensive, intense photocoagulation may lead to massive chorioretinal edema and resultant serous retinal and choroidal detachment. Photocoagulation may precipitate tears of the pigment epithelium. Neither of these causes vitreous hemorrhage.

pool.q: What sickle cell hemoglobinopathy is most commonly associated with proliferative sickle cell retinopathy?
pool.rationale: Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy occurs most commonly with sickle cell hemoglobin C (SC), at a rate of approximately 33%. It occurs less commonly with sickle cell thalassemia (SThal), at a rate of approximately 14%. Sickle cell homozygote (SS) disease results in more systemic complications but has a very low incidence of proliferative retinopathy, approximately 3%. Proliferative retinopathy is rare with sickle cell trait (AS).

pool.q: What toxicity is most likely to cause a cherry red spot on fundoscopic exam?
pool.rationale: At toxic levels, quinine can cause retinal ganglion toxicity that produces thickening and opacification of the ganglion cell layer, leading to the appearance of a cherry red spot. With time, inner retinal atrophy and optic atrophy will develop with quinine toxicity. Methanol toxicity can cause transient optic nerve head edema and macular edema, but the most common sequela of methanol toxicity is optic atrophy. Thioridazine at high doses causes a pigmentary retinopathy, while tamoxifen can induce a crystalline retinopathy.

pool.q: What is the appropriate timing of surgical intervention for hemorrhagic choroidal detachment?

options.c: It is postponed to allow clot liquefaction.

pool.rationale:
Surgical intervention for hemorrhagic choroidal detachments is usually postponed 7 to 10 days to allow for clot liquefaction.
Immediate surgical intervention is not advisable, since the blood clots readily and is not easily drained.
Surgical intervention is required in cases with appositional choroidal detachments, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), or recalcitrant pain.

pool.q: What is the most important risk factor for the development of radiation retinopathy following plaque brachytherapy?

options.a: use of ruthenium-106 or palladium-103 rather than an iodine-125 plaque
options.b: smaller basal diameter and apical height at tumor presentation
options.c: total radiation dose greater than 30 grays (3000 rads)

pool.rationale: A total radiation dose greater than 30 grays (3000 rads) is a risk factor for the development of radiation retinopathy following plaque brachytherapy. There is no definite difference in the incidence of radiation retinopathy with the use of ruthenium-106, palladium-103, or iodine-125, given equal total dosage. Pre-equatorial plaque placement does not increase the risk of radiation retinopathy, although it may increase the incidence of iris neovascularization and/or cataract. Tumors with a smaller basal diameter and apical height at presentation require a lower radiation dose and therefore potentially have a lower incidence of radiation retinopathy following treatment.

pool.q: What is the most common risk factor for exogenous fungal endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale:
Exogenous fungal endophthalmitis is rare in North America and Europe. In tropical regions, it occurs most commonly following trauma or ocular surgery.
Fungal sepsis, especially in the setting of systemic immunosuppression, can cause endogenous fungal endophthalmitis.
Cocaine abuse is not associated with exogenous fungal endophthalmitis.

pool.q: Choroideremia is transmitted by what mode of inheritance?
pool.rationale: Choroideremia is transmitted by an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance. It is a degeneration of the choriocapillaris of the choroid, and of the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and retina. The disease results in progressive loss of vision, almost exclusively in males. In childhood, night blindness is the most common first symptom. As the disease progresses, vision loss results, frequently starting as an irregular ring that gradually expands both centrally and peripherally. Progression continues throughout the individual's life, where both the rate of change and the degree of visual loss are variable among those affected, even within the same family.

pool.q: Atrophic retinal holes are commonly associated with what condition?
pool.rationale: Atrophic retinal holes are commonly associated with lattice degeneration. They are infrequently the cause of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. They represent atrophic rather than tractional retinal breaks, so they are not caused by posterior vitreous detachment, and they are not associated with vitreous hemorrhage.

pool.q: Verteporfin is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for what indication?

options.d: subfoveal choroidal neovascularization (CNV) secondary to posterior uveitis

pool.rationale: Verteporfin is a photosensitizing drug that is locally activated by laser during photodynamic therapy (PDT). PDT is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in the treatment of subfoveal choroidal neovascularizations (CNVs) associated with AMD, myopia, and presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS). The use of PDT for managing CNV has declined dramatically, given the better success of anti-VEGF agents, but it remains an adjunctive therapy for CNV in some scenarios. PDT is used off-label to treat CSC and circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas.
